A new `device_limit` key is added under `[auth.anonymous]`, but the configuration documentation (configure-security/configure-authentication docs in grafana/grafana) is not updated in this PR, and the PR description still contains unfilled template placeholders ("[Add a description...]", "Fixes #"). Users cannot discover or correctly use the setting, and the intended semantics (0 = unlimited, expiry window of 30 days) are only visible in code.

anonymousDeviceLimit always serialized, contradicting the optional TS type

The Go DTO field `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`, so the frontend settings JSON always contains `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0` when unlimited, while the TypeScript type declares it as `number | undefined`. Code distinguishing "no limit" via `undefined` (e.g. `if (config.anonymousDeviceLimit)`) works, but code using `=== undefined` or relying on the key's absence will misbehave. The Go field should be a pointer with `omitempty` (like `TokenExpirationDayLimit`-style optional fields) to match the declared contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug/progress logging emitted at Error level with always-nil error field

The new batch loops call r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...) (and similarly at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) unconditionally, even on the success path. These are informational/progress messages about normal cleanup batches, but they log at Error level, which will fire alerting and pollute error-level logs on every cleanup run for every Grafana instance with annotation cleanup enabled. Additionally, the "err" key is logged after the `if err != nil` early-return, so it is always nil. These should be Debug-level logs and the nil err fields removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job frequency changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without description or release note

The ticker driving all background cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) was changed from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. This is a significant, unrelated behavioral change that is not mentioned in the PR description or tied to the deadlock fix, and it multiplies the background DB load of all cleanup jobs by ~10x. If the 1-minute cadence is intentionally needed for the new batched annotation cleanup, it should be documented in the PR/What's New; otherwise it should be reverted or made configurable.

false_positives.candidate:
untilDoneOrCancelled can loop forever when fetched IDs delete zero rows

The batching loop terminates only when a batch reports zero affected rows (or errors/context cancel). There is now a divergence between the SELECT (fetchIDs) and the DELETE (deleteByIDs) since they run in separate sessions: if fetchIDs keeps returning the same IDs but the DELETE affects 0 rows (e.g., rows concurrently deleted by another process, or RowsAffected misreporting on some drivers), the loop never terminates and spins on the same query forever. Previously the delete affected-rows and selection were one statement so this could not happen. A safer termination condition is len(ids) == 0, not affected == 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one

In `Delete`, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base `d.Log` rather than the locally built `log` (with name/kind/method values) that every other method uses. Any logger retrieved from the context downstream (including in the async legacy goroutine, which inherits this ctx) will be missing the name and kind fields, making log correlation for deletes inconsistent.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection async legacy call records metric as 'storage' duration

In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the legacy delete result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. This pollutes the `unified_storage_write_duration`/legacy metric series with legacy-store latencies and error counts, making the dual-writer metrics wrong and misleading for anyone monitoring migration progress.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric uses object name instead of kind as label

On the Delete success path, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the resource `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind` as the label. Since object names are unbounded user-controlled values, this creates unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus (one metric series per deleted object name) and inconsistent labeling versus the failure path on line 103. It should pass `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes

In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to the legacy store derives its 10-second-timeout context from the incoming request context (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The parent `ctx` is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request that triggered the write completes, so the legacy write is very likely aborted immediately rather than running for the intended 10 seconds. This defeats the purpose of the 'safe measure' write to legacy: legacy storage will silently miss writes whenever the client disconnects or the request handler returns quickly, leaving the two stores permanently divergent with no error surfaced. The goroutine should use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context) as the parent.

No retry, queue, or error surfacing for failed legacy writes

All legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines: if `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete` fails (or the derived context is cancelled per the context issue), the error is only swallowed into a metric — there is no logging of the failure, no retry, and no reconciliation mechanism. Once mode 3 is the default, any transient legacy failure leaves the legacy database permanently out of sync, which matters because legacy Grafana APIs and other code paths still read from legacy storage. At minimum the goroutines should log the legacy error, and the team should confirm a backfill/reconciliation job exists before enabling mode 3.

Storage failures recorded under the legacy metric in Create and Update

In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129), the error path when the unified Storage call fails calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. This records a failed, zero-length 'legacy' operation that never happened, corrupting legacy-store error-rate and duration metrics. It should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` to match the Delete and DeleteCollection error paths.

Tests spawn unmocked async legacy calls that can panic or race in goroutines

Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a background goroutine, but the tests never wait for it and in several success cases never stub it: TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection set up no `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection` mock expectations, and TestMode3_Create's second case stubs only the legacy mock. testify's `mock.Mock` panics on calls to methods with no expected call, so these goroutines can panic non-deterministically after the subtest finishes, causing flaky suite crashes. Additionally, since the goroutine's error is never returned or awaited, no test actually verifies that the legacy write happens, times out, or that legacy failures are correctly logged/metriced — the core behavior of this PR is untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed reload overwrites a previously valid cache entry with nil

When GetWebAssets fails to load the manifest (result == nil, err != nil), line 69 unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result (nil). In Dev mode, where reloads are attempted on every call, a transient read failure of assets-manifest.json discards a previously cached, still-valid *dtos.EntryPointAssets, so subsequent requests also fail until the file loads again. Consider only overwriting the cache when err == nil.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-nil result can be returned together with a non-nil error

In the CDN branch, readWebAssetsFromCDN can return both a non-nil dto and a non-nil error (e.g. if the HTTP request succeeds but SetContentDeliveryURL or a later step fails, or if the decoder returns partial data and an error). In that case the file-read fallback at line 59 is skipped (result != nil), and GetWebAssets returns a valid-looking result alongside an error. Callers that check err first will treat this as a failure, while callers that check the pointer will use a possibly malformed asset list. The code should decide on a single source of truth (either result or err) before caching and returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has dead/misleading logic and ignores the feature flag entirely

The function reads `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false in both branches, so it always returns false regardless of the flag. If intentionally disabling the feature, the function should simply return false (or be removed and the check inlined); as written it implies the flag is consulted when it is not, which will confuse future maintainers re-enabling the feature (they will flip the flag expecting it to work).

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TablesList is now guaranteed to fail and still contains the SQL-string-formatting code

TablesList calls NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, which now always returns errors.New("not implemented"), so TablesList can never succeed. The function (including the `fmt.Sprintf` SQL string interpolation it was built around) is effectively dead code reached only via UnmarshalSQLCommand to produce a generic error. It should either be removed or its callers short-circuited so users get a meaningful error.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and unhelpful

When a user submits a SQL expression (even one that was previously working with the feature toggle enabled), they get "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is implemented but disabled; a message like "SQL expressions are disabled" would be accurate and actionable. As written, users and support will misdiagnose the cause.

Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not gated by the disable check

ReadQuery now returns early for QueryTypeSQL, but the rawNode-based UnmarshalSQLCommand path still constructs a SQLCommand without any feature check. Since sql.TablesList now calls the stub DB which always returns "not implemented", users going through that path get an opaque "error reading SQL command" bad-request error instead of a clear 'feature disabled' message. The gating is inconsistent between the two parsing paths; both should be disabled the same way.

No tests cover the new disabled-SQL behavior

The PR changes the behavior of SQL expressions (they now always error) and adds an enableSqlExpressions helper whose return value must stay false for the CVE fix to hold, yet no test is added asserting that a SQL expression query returns an error regardless of the FlagSqlExpressions toggle state. Without a regression test, a future refactor of this confusing helper could silently re-enable the vulnerable code path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the whole-function lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, which (coarsely) serialized index creation. With the lock now only taken around the final map write, two concurrent callers (e.g. two gRPC Search requests hitting getOrCreateIndex for the same NamespacedResource, or a watch event arriving during a first search) can both observe GetIndex()==nil and both run BuildIndex for the same key. For file-based indexes both will call bleve.New with the same directory (filepath.Join(Root, namespace, resource.group)); the second call fails or clobbers the first, and the cache ends up with one index while the other caller holds a stale index object that will never receive watch updates. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go already has a TODO acknowledging the per-key blocking need; the lock removal makes this a live bug rather than a theoretical one. A per-key singleflight/mutex is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache without the cache lock while BuildIndex writes it

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no cacheMu protection. BuildIndex now writes to b.cache (b.cache[key] = idx) concurrently with index builds running in parallel from init's errgroup workers. Previously the coarse lock at least serialized map writes across all builds; now an unsynchronized map read concurrent with a map write can panic the process with 'concurrent map read and map write' or return inconsistent totals. Take b.cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.

false_positives.candidate:
Goroutine writes to shared err variable raced by main test goroutine

The goroutine launched at line 50 assigns to the outer err variable (err = ms.Run()), while the main test goroutine subsequently reads and reassigns the same err at lines 59-62 (client.Get, res.Body.Close) and again in require.NoError. This is a data race that can also cause a require.NoError on line 60 to see the 'context canceled' error set by the goroutine during shutdown, producing flaky failures. Use a local variable inside the goroutine.

totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from multiple errgroup goroutines without synchronization

In searchSupport.init, each group.Go closure does totalBatchesIndexed++ on a plain int shared across up to s.initWorkers concurrent goroutines. This is a data race (undefined behavior; the span attribute 'namespaced_indexed' can be wrong). Use sync/atomic or collect counts per goroutine.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes IDP with literal alias "alias" instead of the created alias

In testCacheIDPForLogin, after creating each IDP the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` — the string literal "alias" is used instead of the variable `alias` ("idp-alias-" + i). The cleanup therefore targets a non-existent resource, so none of the 21 IDPs created by the test are ever removed. Consequences: leaked identity providers accumulate in the test realm across test methods (the same test class runs other tests against the same realm), which can break subsequent assertions that count providers, and the cleanup call itself may throw a 404 when executed. The same bug exists at line 425 for the "idp-alias-20" provider. The fix is `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove);`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin cache hit can return IDPs whose organization-aware enabled state differs from the cached list

The cached getForLogin result stores only internal IDs and re-fetches each IDP via session.identityProviders().getById(id), which returns the organization-aware wrapper. For an IDP linked to an organization that has since been disabled, the cached login list still contains it and only the consumer-side isEnabled() re-check (added in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean) filters it out. Any other caller of getForLogin that does not re-check isEnabled (the SPI contract says results are "suitable for being displayed in the login pages") will get disabled-org brokers from the cache. Disabling/removing an organization does not invalidate the cacheKeyForLogin entries, only IDP CRUD does. At minimum the contract should be documented, or the org disablement path should invalidate the login caches.

registerIDPInvalidation NPEs when the IDP model is null (remove of unknown/nonexistent alias)

In remove(), `storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` can be null when no IDP with that alias exists; the code then unconditionally calls `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` (null-safe via the Objects::nonNull predicate), but the pre-existing `registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp)` path at line 103 dereferences it (`idp.getInternalId()`), throwing a NullPointerException on remove of an unknown alias. While the null-deref itself predates this PR for the invalid-cache branch, the change now also makes the delegate lookup happen on every remove, so any caller removing a nonexistent alias hits it. A null guard in registerIDPInvalidation (or before calling it) is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default JKS KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider

The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is the Sun provider (for "pkcs12"/"jks"), not BouncyCastle. The interface contract ("@return BouncyCastle security provider") is violated, and any code path in keycloak-core/authz-client that calls `CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider()` expecting BC-specific behavior (e.g. algorithms only BC provides, or null-check semantics used by WildFlyElytronProvider consumers) will silently get a wrong provider. Either return null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does when no BC is available) or document why the default keystore provider is acceptable here.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates and discards encoder objects

Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build two encoders whose results are thrown away; only the `writeDerSeq` chain on lines 117-121 is used. This is leftover debugging/dead code that allocates needless objects on every signature conversion and confuses readers into thinking those calls have an effect. The two lines should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence() silently accepts indefinite-length encodings and returns an empty list

When readLength() encounters the indefinite-length marker 0x80 it returns -1; readSequence()'s `while (length > 0)` loop then never executes and an empty list is returned without consuming any content octets. Callers like asn1derToConcatenatedRS will only detect this indirectly via the size!=2 check, but any future caller iterating the returned list would treat a malformed BER indefinite-length sequence as a valid empty sequence instead of receiving an error. Indefinite length should be rejected explicitly (it is not valid DER).

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as abstract method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations

The new `int order()` method on the public `CryptoProvider` interface has no default implementation. Any existing external implementation of `CryptoProvider` (e.g. custom providers used by downstream projects or the adapter SPI consumers) will fail to load at runtime once keycloak-common is upgraded: ServiceLoader instantiation throws ServiceConfigurationError with AbstractMethodError on first call to order(), or the class no longer compiles. Since CryptoProvider already uses `default` methods elsewhere in this same interface (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes), `order()` should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) to preserve binary and source compatibility.

false_positives.candidate:
integerToBytes silently truncates out-of-range signature integers

In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes keeps only the low `qLength` bytes when the decoded BigInteger is longer than the expected half-signature length (`qLength < bytes.length` branch takes the *last* bytes of toByteArray(), which for a positive value drops the most significant bytes). A DER signature whose r or s exceeds the curve order would be silently accepted and mangled rather than rejected, producing a signature that could verify against a different value than what was signed in length-mismatch scenarios. Validation (throwing when the value does not fit in qLength) would be the safe behavior for signature conversion.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission finds no per-client resources and leaks the type-level resource name

getClientsWithPermission lists resources via resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...). However, per-client resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) without setting a type, so they are not returned by a type query; the only resource that carries type 'Clients' is the type-level resource created in init(). Consequently the method (a) fails to return the IDs of clients that have per-client permissions granted, and (b) adds the name 'Clients' (the type-level resource name, not a client ID) to the result set when a type-level permission matches, which consumers will treat as a client ID. Either set the resource type when creating per-client resources, or query by name and filter out the type-level resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE risk when falling back to the all-clients resource in hasPermission(ClientModel, String)

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...), which can return null (e.g. when admin permissions are disabled for the realm, or when the type-level resource has not been created). The very next line then calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) with a null resource, which will throw a NullPointerException (or behave unpredictably) instead of returning false. Any admin API call guarded by canManage/canView/canConfigure on a client can therefore fail with a 500 instead of a clean authorization denial.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: getEvaluationContext is unused and canExchangeTo is unimplemented

The private method getEvaluationContext (lines 262-272) is never referenced anywhere in the class; it appears to be a leftover from token-exchange support. Together with the unused imports (Scope, EvaluationContext, TOKEN_EXCHANGE constant, and the unused logger), it suggests token-exchange evaluation was intended but canExchangeTo just throws UnsupportedOperationException. If token exchange for clients is not supported in V2 yet, the dead code should be removed; if it was intended to work, canExchangeTo throwing UnsupportedOperationException is a functional regression versus V1 for realms that enable the V2 feature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Client-removed listener can throw UnsupportedOperationException when V2 feature is enabled

registerListener now gates the event handling on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) and then calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). But management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 (and thus ClientPermissionsV2) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported in V2'). When both features are enabled (V2 is a preview feature that can coexist with V1), deleting any client (or removing a role/group) will trigger this listener and throw an UnsupportedOperationException inside the removal flow, breaking client/role/group deletion.

Per-client resource shadows the all-clients permission fallback

hasPermission(ClientModel, String) only falls back to the type-level 'Clients' resource when resourceStore.findByName returns null for the client's own resource. If a per-client resource exists (e.g. created earlier by a view-only permission) but no permission on it grants the requested scope, the type-level (all clients) permission is never evaluated. An admin who was granted 'manage' on all clients would then be denied manage on that specific client simply because some other, narrower permission once referenced it. The two levels should both be evaluated (or the evaluation should check type-level permissions regardless).

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed from 4 to 3, breaking existing scripts

This PR changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 (and reassigns 4 to FEATURE_DISABLED). Any automation or CI/CD pipeline written against the previous release that branches on exit code 4 to detect 'recreate upgrade required' will now silently misinterpret the result: exit code 4 now means the feature is disabled, and recreate is signaled by a different code. Since the whole point of this tool is to be scriptable via exit codes (as documented), this is a breaking contract change for existing consumers. If the renumbering is intentional, it should at least be called out in the PR description/release notes; alternatively pick an unused code (e.g. 5) for FEATURE_DISABLED to preserve compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION claims the Operator fails without the rolling-updates feature, but the default strategy is documented as usable

The added CAUTION states 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail.' However the same section documents that the default (`<not set>`) strategy mimics Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior, and the accompanying UpgradeTest only enables the rolling-updates feature when a strategy is explicitly set (updateStrategy != null). This means the operator does not fail for the default strategy without the feature, contradicting the CAUTION. The doc should clarify that the feature is required only when spec.update is configured (e.g. with an explicit strategy), otherwise users following the doc will enable the feature unnecessarily or distrust the doc after observing the default path works without it.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert the new exit code 4

The new test testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message but not the process exit code. The feature-disabled path introduces a new documented exit code (4), which is the primary machine-readable contract of this tool. A regression that prints the message but exits with the wrong code (e.g. 1 or 0) would not be caught. The test should assert result.exitCode() == 4, as the other tests assert exit codes explicitly (e.g. testCompatible asserts 0).

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Global canManage() grants manage rights to admins holding only the VIEW scope on all groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (no-arg) falls back to `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. Since hasPermission returns true if ANY of the listed scopes is granted, an admin who only has the `view` scope on the all-groups resource passes canManage(). This method backs `auth.groups().requireManage()`, which guards group creation (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup) and other write paths, so a view-only fine-grained admin can create/modify top-level groups — a privilege escalation. The same pattern does not exist for users (UserPermissions.canManage() only checks MANAGE_SCOPE). The javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() ("permission to VIEW or MANAGE groups") appears to have replicated this mistake rather than describing intended behavior. It should only accept the MANAGE scope, and a negative test (view-only all-groups permission must not allow group creation) should be added.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

false_positives.candidate:
NPE in hasPermission when the group resource and the all-groups resource are both missing

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission, when `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` returns null (no per-group resource exists), the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`. That method returns null when the resource server is not the admin-permissions client or admin permissions are not enabled, and can also simply find no 'Groups' type resource. In that case `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)` and the subsequent `resource.getScopes()` on line 152 will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning false. The null case must be handled (return false), as done implicitly by the early null checks in the V1 GroupPermissions.hasPermission.

No negative test that a VIEW-only all-groups permission does not grant manage operations

testManageAllGroups only verifies that MANAGE on all-groups enables group creation/update, but there is no test asserting that an admin holding only the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is still forbidden from creating or updating groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup / GroupResource.updateGroup). Because GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope in its fallback (see separate finding), this exact regression is currently unguarded by the test suite; adding such a negative test would catch it.

getResourceName has no Groups handling, so group permission resources display null names

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName special-cases the USERS resource type (returning "All users" or the username) but has no branch for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE. For group policies, it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, and group resources created via getOrCreateResource never set a display name (only name = group id). Any UI/logic that renders policy resources for the admin-permissions client will therefore show a raw group id or null instead of a human-readable group name. A resolveGroup-based branch (mirroring the Users handling) is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Italian text introduced into Lithuanian message files

totpStep1 in the Lithuanian account messages was replaced with 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:' — an Italian sentence. The same Italian text was also put into themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/login/messages/messages_lt.properties (loginTotpStep1, line 71). Lithuanian users will see Italian on the OTP setup page. It should be translated to Lithuanian (e.g. 'Įdiekite vieną iš šių programėlių į savo mobilųjį telefoną:').

false_negatives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.

The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
English-file path rewriting is wrong for community-only theme directories, causing the verifier to fail

The English reference file is computed as file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties"). This only works for files under themes/src/main/resources-community whose English counterpart exists under themes/src/main/resources. For the JS themes (js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources-community and js/apps/account-ui/maven-resources-community) there is no sibling "maven-resources" directory containing the _en file in the community repository, so the English bundle cannot be loaded and the verifier throws a RuntimeException (see other finding) for every such file. Additionally, many community-only locales (e.g. messages_ca, messages_ka under resources-community) have no _en-independent counterpart issue but product resources may lack them too; any locale file whose English file does not exist at the rewritten path will crash the verification rather than being skipped or reported.

Java MessageFormat choice syntax is not supported by the account UI's JS i18n stack

error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed from 'Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).' to 'Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.'. The keycloak.v3 account theme is a React app whose message properties use double-brace interpolation ({{0}}, {{1}} everywhere else in this file). The single-brace Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat syntax is not evaluated by that JS i18n stack, so users of the account console will likely see the literal string '{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}' (and possibly un-interpolated {0}/{1}/{2}) instead of a pluralized message. The same change is made in js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources-community/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties (error-invalid-multivalued-size) which is also a React (i18next) UI. The choice format is correct only for the server-side FreeMarker themes (themes/src/main/resources...), where those files were updated consistently.

PropertyResourceBundle reads the file as ISO-8859-1 while the duplicate-key check uses UTF-8

verifyNoDuplicateKeys reads the file via Files.readString (UTF-8), but verifySafeHtml loads the same file with new PropertyResourceBundle(new FileInputStream(file)), and PropertyResourceBundle(Properties.load(InputStream)) decodes as ISO-8859-1. These message files are UTF-8 (Arabic, Chinese, Thai, etc.), so the values used for HTML comparison will be mojibake. In most cases value and sanitized are corrupted identically so the comparison still passes, but any character whose UTF-8 bytes contain 0x3C ('<') or 0x26 ('&') in a trailing byte after ISO-8859-1 decoding can produce spurious 'Illegal HTML' findings or, worse, hide real differences. The bundle should be loaded with an InputStreamReader specifying UTF-8.

containsHtml only recognizes lowercase tags, so uppercase HTML in the English source disables HTML in translations HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>") only matches lowercase tag names. If an English source string contained e.g. '
' or '

' (case-insensitive HTML is legal), containsHtml() returns false and POLICY_NO_HTML is used, while the OWASP sanitizer strips tags case-insensitively — a translation carrying the same uppercase tag would be flagged, and one with lowercase variants would be inconsistently treated. Use (?i) in the pattern.

verifySafeHtml throws raw RuntimeException, crashing the build instead of reporting a message

When the derived English reference file cannot be opened (see separate finding), or the current file cannot be re-read, verifySafeHtml throws a plain RuntimeException. The surrounding verify() method only catches IOException and wraps it into a MojoExecutionException; an uncaught RuntimeException will propagate out of the mojo and abort the build with a stack trace rather than being added to the reported `messages` list. A verification tool should report the problem as a message (or wrap it in MojoExecutionException) so users get a readable diagnostic.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rawTokenId null check is missing (duplicated grantType check)

The constructor contains `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, ...)` twice; the second occurrence was meant to be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`. As a result a null rawTokenId is silently accepted and will later produce a token ID like 'onrtac:null' when encoded, instead of failing fast.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted comparison and wrong index

The new matcher returns false when the grant shortcut MATCHES the expected value: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. This inverts the logic, so a correctly encoded token ID (e.g. 'onrtac:<uuid>') will fail the matcher while wrong grant types pass (as long as the UUID part is valid). Additionally the comment and the encoding format say the grant shortcut occupies characters 4-5 (substring(4,6)), but the code reads substring(3,5), which is the second char of token type plus first char of grant shortcut. Every test using expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken will assert against the wrong characters with inverted semantics.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Duplicate-shortcut validation is bypassed by lazy map refresh

postInit validates that no two grant types share a shortcut by comparing map sizes, but getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut later lazily insert entries into the ConcurrentHashMaps without any collision check. If a custom grant deployed at runtime has the same shortcut as a built-in grant (e.g. 'ac'), its mapping silently overwrites the built-in one in grantsByShortcuts, causing decode of existing token IDs to resolve the wrong grant type. The lazy path should detect that the shortcut is already mapped to a different grant and fail (or refuse to register), preserving the invariant enforced at startup.

Grant type attribute on refresh overwrites original grant context permanently for the client session

validateToken sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, REFRESH_TOKEN)` on the (reused) client session context before recreating the token. If the same client session is later used to mint another token through a different path that does not set the attribute (e.g. another grant implementation or token exchange path that relies on the original value), it will now incorrectly encode 'refresh_token' as the grant. Every token minted after the first refresh will report grant type 'refresh_token' instead of the grant that originally authenticated the session, losing the information this PR intends to preserve. If that is intended semantics it should be documented; otherwise the original grant should be retained and only the refresh-time token flagged.

Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed, breaking API for custom grants

The PR removes the public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor from the non-internal `OAuth2GrantType.Context` class (server-spi-private is part of Keycloak's provider API). Any existing third-party OAuth2GrantType implementation that used this constructor to clone the context (e.g. to override formParams) will fail to compile/deploy after upgrade. This is an API/contract break that should either be deprecated instead of removed, or noted as an intentional incompatible change with migration documentation.

decode error message says 'Expected length of 6' but refers to encoded context length

When the prefix before ':' is not exactly 6 chars the code throws "Incorrect token id: '...'. Expected length of 6." — ambiguous/wrong message since it is the encoded context part, not the token id, that must be 6 characters. A caller reading the message with a 43-char token ID will be confused. Minor but worth fixing while the format is new.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials() returns a freshly generated credential id on every call and drops the stored one; NPE for unknown user

In getCredentials(), the recovery-codes CredentialModel is rebuilt via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...), which generates a new random id each call instead of returning myUser.recoveryCodes with its stored id. Consequently the credential id reported to Keycloak is unstable (changes between calls), so operations like deleting the credential by id via the account REST endpoint (as the existing OTP test does) cannot work for recovery codes, and the stored id set in updateCredential() is effectively unused. Also, getMyUser(user) may return null for an unknown user and myUser.recoveryCodes would throw an NPE instead of returning an empty stream. Additionally, disableCredentialType() does not handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE even though supportsCredentialType() advertises it, so disabling recovery codes through the admin REST API silently logs 'unsupported' and leaves the credential in place — none of these paths are covered by the new test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Creating recovery codes in user storage leaves a pre-existing local recovery credential active

createRecoveryCodesCredential() first tries user.credentialManager().updateCredential(); if the user storage accepts the recovery-codes type it stores the credential there and returns, never removing any previously stored local (Keycloak DB) recovery-code credential for that user. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential() path replaces the existing credential, so the previous behavior guaranteed a single active credential. With this change a user who already had a local recovery credential and whose storage now supports the type ends up with two simultaneously valid recovery-code credentials (one local, one federated), and the old one is never invalidated. The user-storage branch should also remove any stored local credential of the same type (or the check should be skipped when a local credential exists).

Exhausted federated recovery-code credential cannot be removed via removeStoredCredentialById

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, an unhealthy process is `process.kill()`-ed and a replacement is immediately started via `_create_process_for_shards`, but the old process object is never `join()`-ed. In production (spawn mode) each killed process becomes a zombie until the parent exits, and its `SpansBuffer` (with its Redis connection pool) is dropped from `self.buffers[process_index]` without being closed, leaking connections. Since restarts can happen repeatedly (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index), a consumer running for a long time can accumulate zombies and leaked Redis connections. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, a process that legitimately crashed 11 times over months of uptime (e.g. transient Redis outages) will cause `_ensure_processes_alive` to raise RuntimeError and take down the whole consumer. The counter should be reset once the replacement process has been observed healthy for some period. `test_basic` sets `current_drift` and then sleeps for 0.1s before `step.join()`, expecting the background flusher thread to have picked up the new drift and flushed the segment. There is no synchronization guaranteeing the thread reached the read of `current_drift` or completed the flush/produce within 100ms, so the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking can flake on slow/loaded CI. A poll-until-assertion loop (with timeout) would make this deterministic.

false_positives.candidate:
queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown require Python 3.13

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, but Queue.shutdown() and the ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs (3.11/3.12) this raises AttributeError at shutdown time (silently swallowed by the try/except, so workers are never told to stop and blocked worker threads never exit), and the `except queue.ShutDown` handlers would fail to even import-resolve at runtime. The graceful shutdown path is broken on supported Python versions; use a sentinel/Event-based approach instead.

Failed messages are marked completed and their offsets committed, silently dropping them

OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a `finally` block, so when result_processor raises, the offset is still considered complete and the commit loop will commit past it. Combined with the fact that ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows all exceptions (logs only), any message that fails processing (e.g. DB error, bad subscription data) is permanently lost with no retry and no DLQ — the offset is committed so it will never be redelivered. The existing test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts this drop-on-failure behavior. There should be a retry/DLQ path or the offset should remain outstanding (blocking commit) on failure so the message is redelivered.

Queues are unbounded — no backpressure despite docstring claim, risk of unbounded memory growth

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after enqueueing, so the arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as it can. If processing (DB-backed result handling) is slower than consumption, queues grow without limit, holding decoded messages and their Message objects in memory until OOM. The class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' guarantee is false as implemented. Either set maxsize and block/propagate backpressure in submit(), or bound total in-flight items.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain, losing final offset commits

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(), which is what drains the worker queues. Any messages processed after the last commit-loop iteration (up to the entire remaining queue contents at shutdown) will be processed but never committed. On restart/rebalance those messages are redelivered and reprocessed, which for non-idempotent result handling means duplicate side effects. The correct order is: stop accepting new work, drain queues, do a final get_committable_offsets/commit, then stop the commit thread.

join() unconditionally calls close(), causing double shutdown and ignoring its timeout

Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close() then join() on strategies. Here join() calls close() again: shutdown_event.set() and commit_thread.join() are harmless, but queue_pool.shutdown() runs a second time — each Queue.shutdown() (on 3.13) raises ValueError on already-shutdown queues (swallowed by the broad except, hiding errors), and worker.join() is called again. Additionally the `timeout` parameter of join() is accepted but never used, so a stuck worker blocks shutdown for the full 5s join regardless. join() should simply wait (using its timeout) for work to drain, not re-run shutdown.

Worker thread death permanently stalls offset commits for its queue

If an OrderedQueueWorker thread exits for any reason other than a clean shutdown — e.g. an exception raised by metrics.gauge or the sentry_sdk transaction wrapper inside the finally block, or a non-Exception BaseException from result_processor — the thread dies, but all offsets of items still sitting in its queue remain in OffsetTracker.outstanding forever. get_committable_offsets will never advance past the smallest such offset, so commits for that partition stop entirely, backpressure-free consumption continues enqueueing into a queue nobody reads, and memory grows until the process is killed. There is no liveness check or worker restart.

Arroyo Commit callable invoked from a background thread concurrently with the consumer thread

The commit loop thread calls the arroyo Commit function (which ends up calling consumer commit / interacting with consumer state) once per second, while the StreamProcessor's main thread concurrently polls the consumer and may itself commit or rebalance. Arroyo strategies normally call commit from the processing (main) thread; calling it from an unsynchronized background thread risks racing with the consumer during rebalances/shutdown and can produce errors or commits of stale offsets. This needs verification against arroyo's thread-safety contract, or the commit should be marshalled back to the strategy thread (e.g. via poll()).

test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to salted string hashing

The test asserts that 20 arbitrary group keys hashed with Python's builtin hash() (which is salted per process for str) land on exactly all 3 queues. With random salt it is possible (though unlikely) that fewer than 3 distinct indices are hit, making the test flaky across runs. Asserting `>= 2` or using fixed deterministic keys would be robust.

A sentry_sdk transaction is started for every single message in every worker

OrderedQueueWorker wraps each individual result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction. At production uptime-result volumes this creates and discards a transaction object per message (20 queues × full throughput), adding significant per-message overhead and, if any transaction sampling is enabled, flooding Sentry with events. The batched-parallel mode wraps batches, not items; this should be a span or sampled/omitted entirely.

The script now calls `zcard`/`zunionstore` where it previously called `scard`/`sunionstore`. During a rolling deploy, old-version processes still write span payloads via `sadd`/`sunionstore` while new-version processes read them with `zcard`, so existing set-typed keys are invisible to the new logic (`zcard` on a set key returns a WRONGTYPE error in Redis, actually failing the EVALSHA call entirely). If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with `set_span_id` pointing at an intermediate node and the span is written to the wrong buffer key, splitting a segment — silently, since the returned `redirect_depth` metric is the only signal. If this reduction was intentional (e.g. to bound Redis script runtime), it should be documented and covered by a test; neither exists.

A new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter changes which paginator implementation and behavior (including negative-offset support) the audit log endpoint uses, but it is not documented in the API schema, not covered by any endpoint test, and the behavior difference is invisible to clients. The call passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to `self.paginate(...)`. If it does not forward the kwarg, this raises a TypeError (500) on every optimized request; if it does forward it, the default `enable_advanced_features=False` still enables the negative-offset branch only for this flag combination, which no test exercises. The core behavioral changes of this PR — segments exceeding 1000 spans being truncated via `zpopmin`, the removal of the `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data`, and the set→sorted-set conversion — have no test coverage.
