Clicking it fires `removeMember`, which the server rejects with 422 ("can not modify automatic"), producing a silently failing/confusing action with no user-facing error handling (there is no failure handler on `removeMember` in the model or controller).

add_members silently ignores non-existent usernames and reports success

`add_members` iterates the submitted usernames and only adds users found via `User.find_by_username`, but if a username doesn't match any user it is silently skipped and the endpoint still returns `success_json`. The admin UI then reloads the member list and gives the operator no indication that some (or all) of the requested members were not added — typos appear to succeed. The endpoint should report which usernames could not be found so the client can surface an error.

create drops the alias_level parameter the client sends

The new `Discourse.Group#create` (app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js) posts `asJSON()` which includes `alias_level`, but the server's `create` action only assigns `name` and `visible`; `alias_level` is never read. A newly created group therefore always gets the default alias level regardless of what the admin selected in the form, and the value is only applied later if the admin saves again. `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i if params[:alias_level].present?` should also be applied in `create`.

members endpoint accepts an unbounded limit parameter

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` is passed straight into `group.users.limit(limit)` with no maximum cap and no guard against nonsense values. Any client (this is a public, non-admin endpoint) can request `/groups/<name>/members.json?limit=1000000` and force serialization of the group's entire membership in one request, which on large groups (e.g. trust_level_0) is an expensive query and serialization. A sane cap such as `[limit, 1000].min` (and flooring at 0) should be enforced.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a DB write inside model validation

BlockedEmail.should_block? is invoked from EmailValidator.validate_each, i.e. from within ActiveRecord validation of a User. It increments match_count and calls record.save on the BlockedEmail row as a side effect of validating another model. This means every failed signup attempt (including repeated retries of the same form) triggers a write, the increment is a read-modify-write race under concurrency (lost updates on match_count/last_match_at), and if the BlockedEmail save fails (e.g. stale record) the method silently continues. Statistics tracking should be done outside the validation path, or via an atomic UPDATE (update_counters / SQL increment).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying issue: the query/check method (`BlockedEmail.should_block?` / `should_block_email?`) causes side effects by writing statistics (`match_count` / `last_match_at`) to the database during a read operation, which leads to race conditions in concurrent environments.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) queries `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` with the exact string passed in, but email addresses elsewhere in the app are normalized (e.g. UsersController#change_email uses Email.downcase, and users may sign up with mixed case). A blocked address stored as 'bad@spam.com' will not match a signup using 'Bad@Spam.com', so the block list can be bypassed simply by varying case. The lookup (and the unique index/uniqueness validation) should compare downcased emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is case-sensitive, which allows attackers to bypass the block list by varying the casing of the email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocked-email check applied to existing users changing email, with no admin path to manage block list

The email:true validation runs whenever email_changed? on any User, so an existing (possibly long-standing) member whose address appears in the blocked_emails table can no longer save any change that touches email, and their email changes are rejected with a generic 'is not allowed' message. There is also no admin interface, seed, or API anywhere in this PR that ever creates BlockedEmail records, so the block list cannot be populated and the feature (and its match_count statistics) is effectively dead code as shipped.

rejectedEmails comparison is case-sensitive against server-echoed value

On a failed signup, the email echoed back in result.values.email is pushed into rejectedEmails, and emailValidation checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` with an exact string comparison. If the user retypes the same address with different casing or surrounding whitespace, the client-side rejection is skipped and the form is resubmitted to the server, which rejects it again — the user gets no inline feedback explaining the email is blocked. Normalizing both sides (trim/lowercase) before comparing would make the client check reliable.

Blocked email is reported to user as 'invalid'

When a signup fails because the email is on the server's block list, the client shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid'), i.e. a malformed-address message, rather than a message explaining the address is not permitted (the server has user.email.blocked for this). The user is told their syntactically valid email is invalid, which is confusing and wrong.

Failed-signup response echoes submitted name/username/email back to the client

The create failure path now returns `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to any anonymous requester. Combined with the CSRF skip on create (`skip_before_filter :verify_authenticity_token, only: [:create]`), this endpoint can be probed without a valid token and used as an oracle to enumerate which emails are blocked/blacklisted or already registered, and reflects attacker-controlled input back. Consider not echoing the submitted values (the client already knows what it submitted).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin mixes 2009 and 2012 spec syntaxes that don't work together

The `order($val)` mixin emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` (2009 spec, integer-only, works only alongside `display: -webkit-box`) together with `-ms-flex-order`/`order`. In the corresponding layout files, `flexbox()` is applied to one element and `order(2)`/`order(3)` to different elements (.extra-info-wrapper, .panel), so within any single legacy engine only one of the pair of declarations applies and the reordering silently does nothing; also the 2009 engines require the group values to start at 1 (order 0 default vs. 2/3 here is fine, but the emitted 2009 declarations have no matching old-spec box on the sibling items). Practically this means visual order of the header contents differs between legacy and modern browsers; if legacy engines are not targeted, the 2009-era prefixes should be dropped from these mixins to avoid a false sense of compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly mentions the exact technical limitation described in the golden comment: that `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` (the 2009 spec) require group values to start at 1 instead of 0, leading to rendering differences in legacy browsers.

false_positives.candidate:
float: right on .small-action button is a no-op now that the parent is a flex container

`.small-action` was changed to `@include flexbox()`, but the `button { float: right; }` rule inside it was kept. Floats are ignored on flex items, so the button (e.g. the 'change owner' / moderation button rendered in small actions) will no longer be pushed to the right edge; it will sit inline after the description as an ordinary flex item. The rule should be replaced with a flex-based right alignment (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button), otherwise the small-action button placement regresses visually on topic pages.

Header right panel loses its right alignment on browsers using the legacy flexbox syntax

The old `float: right` on `.d-header .panel` was replaced with `margin-left: auto`. `margin-left: auto` for end-alignment only works in the modern flexbox model; the 2009 box model that the `flexbox()` mixin also emits (`display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`) does not honor auto margins — there you need `-webkit-box-pack: end` on the container. On any browser that only supports the old syntax (older Android/Safari that the prefixes were presumably added for), the login/sign-up panel will sit immediately after the title instead of being right-aligned, and since the floats were removed there is no fallback. Either add the box-pack fallback or keep a float-based fallback.

Removal of .title float leaves no layout for browsers without flexbox support

The diff deletes the `.d-header .contents .title { float: left; }` rule and replaces the layout entirely with the flexbox mixins on `.contents`. Browsers that support none of the five `display` variants emitted by `flexbox()` will fall back to block layout, where the title, extra-info and panel will each stack on their own line instead of laying out horizontally. If those browsers matter, a float fallback should be retained; otherwise the extra prefixed values serve no purpose.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking hidden TL0 profile data

The serializer defines `untrusted_attributes` to hide `website` (and bio, location, etc.) for TL0 users viewed anonymously, but the new `website_name` attribute was only added to the plain `attributes` list. As a result, when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true, the JSON omits `website` but still includes `website_name`, which now (when the website domain matches the instance domain) contains the full URL path. This leaks exactly the information the untrusted-attribute restriction is meant to hide, and it bypasses the existing spec at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11-15 which only checks the enumerated attribute list. `website_name` should be added to `untrusted_attributes` (and a test added).

website_name drops query string and fragment from the URL

When the website domain matches the instance domain, `website_name` is built as `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path`, discarding the query string and fragment. A profile website like `http://example.com/page?id=42` would be displayed as `example.com/page`, so the shown 'complete URL path' is wrong/incomplete for URLs with query parameters. Use `URI(website.to_s).request_uri` or `[path, query].compact.join('?')` instead.

Domain-matching logic misses websites on subdomains of the instance domain

The elsif branch only compares hosts when the label counts are equal and greater than 2, and the else branch only matches when the instance hostname ends with `.#{website_host}` (i.e. the website is a parent of the instance). A website on a subdomain of the instance domain, e.g. website `http://sub.forums.example.com/page` on instance `forums.example.com`, falls through to the else branch where the ends_with check fails, so only the bare host is shown even though it is under the same registrable domain and the PR's intent ('same domain') would suggest showing the full path. The three-way string-split comparison is also ad hoc: `a.b.example.com` vs `x.y.example.com` matches (showing full path) while `sub.forums.example.com` vs `forums.example.com` does not, which is inconsistent.

Scheme-less website URLs yield nil website_name while include_website_name stays true

`URI(website.to_s).host` is nil for values like `example.com/user` (no scheme), so `website_name` returns nil, yet `include_website_name` only checks `website.present?` and therefore still emits a `website_name: null` key. The old client-side `website.split("/")[2]` was equally limited, but if the profile website field accepts scheme-less input on any code path, the profile will render no website label at all where it previously showed the raw string in the link/title. Consider normalizing with a scheme before parsing and guarding inclusion on the computed value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Weak origin check on postMessage via substring match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any message whose origin appears anywhere in discourseUrl. E.g. with discourseUrl 'http://meta.discourse.org', a sender at 'http://meta.discourse.org.evil.com' passes the check (its origin string contains the discourseUrl as a substring) and can drive iframe.height with arbitrary values. The check should compare the parsed origin of discourseUrl to e.origin with strict equality.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same vulnerability: the weak origin validation using `indexOf` (substring matching) on `discourseUrl` and `e.origin` which can be bypassed by an attacker.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls methods on i.content without checking presence. Many RSS feeds provide only a description/summary and no content element (simple-rss returns nil for missing tags), so the scheduled job will raise NoMethodError on nil. With `sidekiq_options retry: false` the exception is swallowed and, more importantly, it aborts processing of the remaining feed items in the same run, so topics after the offending item are never imported until the next hour. Guard with `i.content || i.description` or a nil check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `.scrub` on `i.content` when `i.content` might be nil in RSS feeds, and suggests the exact same fix of falling back to `i.description`.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer header injected unescaped into inline JavaScript

The layout embeds `'<%= request.referer %>'` directly inside a <script> block. The referer is an attacker-controlled HTTP header; ensure_embeddable only checks that URI(referer).host equals the configured embeddable_host, so a referer such as `http://<embeddable_host>/';alert(1);//` passes the host check and breaks out of the JS string literal (and `</script>` sequences break out of the script tag entirely), executing arbitrary script in the Discourse iframe origin. The value must be JSON/JS-escaped (e.g. `json_escape`/to_json) and ideally validated as a full origin before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the unescaped interpolation of `request.referer` into inline JavaScript, leading to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

false_positives.candidate:
RSS feed content is stored and rendered as raw HTML without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method: raw_html, which makes Post#cook return raw unchanged (app/models/post.rb line 133). When called from the PollFeed path (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35-36), `contents` is the raw feed item content with only CGI.unescapeHTML applied — no HTML sanitization occurs. The embed view (app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19) then renders these posts with `raw post.cooked`. Any <script>, inline event handlers, or other malicious markup in the external feed is stored verbatim and executed in the Discourse origin for every visitor of the embedded page, allowing a compromised or malicious feed to hijack Discourse sessions/perform CSRF. The import_remote path limits tags/attributes via readability, but the feed path has no such filtering; contents should be sanitized (e.g. via Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

feed_key is dead code; no conditional-fetch deduplication is implemented

The `feed_key` method (used nowhere) and its 'feed-modified:' redis key suggest the intent was to skip polling when the feed has not changed (e.g. via Last-Modified/ETag), but poll_feed unconditionally re-opens the feed URL and re-processes every item every hour. Every existing embed's content is re-fetched/recomputed and each unchanged item still goes through a TopicEmbed lookup and SHA1 comparison; if content SHA matches it is skipped only after the DB read. Either remove the dead method or wire it up to store/compare the feed's modified time so polling is skipped when unchanged.

setnx followed by separate expire is not atomic

retrieved_recently? uses $redis.setnx and then a separate $redis.expire. If the process dies (or redis restarts) between the two calls, the key 'retrieved:<url>' exists with no TTL and permanently blocks retrieval for that embed URL until manual redis intervention. Use a single SET key value EX 60 NX (or setex-style) operation so the TTL is set atomically with the key creation.

Update path crashes if the embedded post has been deleted

On re-import of an existing embed, `post = embed.post` is used without a nil check before `PostRevisor.new(post)` and `embed.update_column`. If the topic's post was deleted (or post_id points to a removed record — the association has no dependent handling and nothing destroys the TopicEmbed when its post is destroyed), the poll job will raise NoMethodError on nil every run for that URL. Guard for a missing post (and consider destroying the TopicEmbed alongside the post).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of self.downsize; first (width/height) form is dead code

The class now defines `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and then redefines `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. Ruby silently discards the first definition (with a 'method redefined' warning in some modes), and both have the same arity so callers passing width and height as separate integers will now hit the second definition and produce a broken dimension string like "640x480" vs "1024-768"-style concatenation issues... concretely, a caller invoking downsize(from, to, 100, 75) now gets dimensions "100" passed to ImageMagick (75 is bound to opts), producing wrong output rather than an error. The two-integer variant should be removed entirely or the definitions merged, not left as shadowed duplicate definitions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice, causing the second definition (taking `dimensions`) to overwrite the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), making the first unreachable and breaking callers using the old signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client-side limit ignores SiteSetting max image/attachment sizes

The client-side upload validation previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'] (i.e. max_image_size_kb / max_attachment_size_kb) but now hardcodes 10MB. This breaks validation in both directions: on sites where the admin set a lower limit (e.g. 4MB), oversized files pass the client check and only fail on the server with a confusing generic error; and the hardcoded 10MB cap cannot be raised by admins. The same hardcode in the 413 handler (line 246) shows users a wrong maximum size in the error message. The stated goal of the PR (allow large images that the server will downsize) is undermined because the client still blocks any image over 10MB and, worse, blocks images over the (possibly small) configured limit that the new server-side downsizing was meant to accept — the client check should be relaxed or removed for images, not fixed at 10MB.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact problem described in the golden comment: replacing `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` with a hardcoded 10MB limit causes divergence from configured settings, including in the 413 error handler.

false_positives.candidate:
In-place downsize: convert is run with input and output as the same file path

OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...) executes ImageMagick's `convert /tmp/xxx /tmp/xxx`, i.e. the source and destination are the same path. ImageMagick reads the input lazily and can truncate/corrupt the file while writing, or fail outright, depending on format and buffering. The result can be a corrupted or zero-byte upload. The downsized output should be written to a separate temp file and then replace the original.

Animated GIFs lose animation and animated path is never selected for uploads

The animated-image branch in OptimizedImage.optimize is chosen only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but `tempfile.path` for an uploaded file is a Tempfile path with no .gif extension (e.g. /tmp/d discourse-upload...). So animated GIFs always go through `convert #{from}[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame, silently destroying animation. Additionally, `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is passed, but the actual check inside optimize tests the file path's extension, not the flag, so the setting has no effect here. Files with no recognizable animation possible (corrupt images) will also make `convert` fail repeatedly (see next finding).

Downsize loop ignores failures and still submits the oversized file

The while loop decrements `attempt` but never checks the return value of OptimizedImage.downsize, which returns false when convert fails (corrupt image, missing ImageMagick, etc.). On failure the file size never changes, so the loop pointlessly shells out 5 times and then passes the still-oversized file to Upload.create_for, which will reject it with a generic error. The loop should break out and fail fast (or surface a clear error) when downsize returns false.

API URL download cap hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

FileHelper.download for API-provided URLs now uses a fixed 10.megabytes cap instead of SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes. On sites where max_image_size_kb (or max_attachment_size_kb) is configured above 10MB, valid API uploads are now truncated/fail at 10MB with no way to configure it; below 10MB, non-image downloads are no longer bounded by the image setting at all. The cap should be derived from the relevant setting (e.g. [max_image_size_kb, max_attachment_size_kb].max) rather than hardcoded.

Downsized image keeps original filename but stored sha/filesize mismatch metadata assumptions

After downsizing, the upload is created with the original `filename` and the new (smaller) tempfile.size, but the content no longer matches the file the user chose; more importantly, uploads of type where FileHelper.is_image? matches by extension (e.g. .svg) will run ImageMagick `convert` on an SVG with "80%" geometry, which either rasterizes the SVG (destroying its vector nature) or fails. SVGs should be excluded from the downsize path the same way OptimizedImage.create_for special-cases .svg.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate: GET /unsubscribe toggles state and crashes when no TopicUser record exists The unsubscribe action performs a state-changing toggle on a plain GET request. Two concrete problems: (1) `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` returns nil when the logged-in user has no topic_users row for that topic (e.g. they received the email via a mention/watch category without ever visiting, or the row was cleaned up); `tu.notification_level` on the next line then raises NoMethodError, producing a 500 instead of a graceful response. It should use TopicUser.change or handle the nil case. (2) Because the toggle is a side effect of a GET, simply refreshing or re-visiting the emailed link flips the user back and forth between muted and regular, and any third-party page can trigger the state change for a logged-in user via an /link (CSRF via GET). The mutation should be a POST/PUT (or done through the Ember route with an explicit action), not performed on every GET.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same nil pointer/NoMethodError bug when no TopicUser record exists (point 1 in the candidate), while also mentioning an additional concern about state-changing GET requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Direct tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

The unsubscribe action sets notification_level directly on the TopicUser AR object and calls save!, instead of using TopicUser.change. TopicUser.change is the canonical path that also stamps notifications_changed_at, notifications_reason_id, publishes the MessageBus notification_level_change event to the user's open tabs, and handles record creation races. Saving directly leaves notifications_changed_at/reason stale and open clients won't see the level change until reload.

unsubscribe_link now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email that sets add_unsubscribe_link without it

The rewritten `unsubscribe_link` locale string now interpolates both %{user_preferences_url} and %{unsubscribe_url}. Email::MessageBuilder#body and #html_part call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args) whenever @opts[:add_unsubscribe_link] is true, but unsubscribe_url is only supplied by UserNotifications#send_notification_email. Any other builder invocation with add_unsubscribe_link: true and no :unsubscribe_url option (other mailers, plugins, or future call sites — and the old spec case before it was patched in this same PR) will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument (or emit a broken literal `%{unsubscribe_url}` link) when building the email. The per-topic sentence should be a separate locale key used only when the URL is present.

No request specs for the unsubscribe controller action or route

The PR adds a new authenticated, state-mutating controller action (topics#unsubscribe) plus two new routes, but includes no request/controller specs covering: the redirect when the slug is missing/mismatched, the toggle behavior at each starting notification level, the nil-TopicUser case, access control for topics the user cannot see, and the logged-out redirect. The only test touched is the message_builder spec, so the most fragile new code (the toggling GET) ships untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no authentication (no webhook secret or signature), so the receiving self-hoster endpoint cannot verify the request actually came from its Cal.com instance, and anyone who can reach the endpoint can request access tokens for arbitrary users. There is also no timeout or non-200 handling — a slow or failing endpoint will hang every booking that triggers a token refresh. Attach the CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header and check the response status before returning.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED depends on CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT too, misleading gating

The flag is true whenever CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY are set, even if CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is empty. In that configuration the webhook is enabled but every refresh call site takes the normal path (each also checks the endpoint separately), which is arguably intended — but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` switches to the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` based on both flag and endpoint while `refreshOAuthTokens` uses the same pair of conditions evaluated at different times, making the behavior inconsistent and hard to reason about. Consolidate the enablement condition (flag + endpoint) into one shared constant so webhook receipt and refresh-path behavior cannot diverge.

Webhook secret compared with strict equality (not timing-safe)

The CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header is compared using `!==`, which is not constant-time. Use a timing-safe comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on digested values) for secret verification, as is standard for webhook endpoints, to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte to an attacker who can make repeated requests.

Missing Content-Type header on the sync POST request

The fetch to the credential sync endpoint sends a `URLSearchParams` body but no `Content-Type` header. While fetch infers `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for URLSearchParams in modern runtimes, the endpoint contract is undocumented and some servers/parsers require the explicit header; a request that the receiving endpoint can't parse will silently break token refresh. Set `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" }` and document the expected request/response contract for self-hosters.

The internal consumer `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`, but `getCalendarCredentials` is an exported function; any other caller that uses `item.calendar` directly (e.g. calling `calendar.listCalendars()` or checking `if (!calendar)`) now operates on a Promise, which is always truthy, so null-checks stop working and method calls will fail at runtime with no TypeScript error if the consumer widened the type. false_positives.candidate:
Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and resources

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, an unhealthy process is `process.kill()`-ed and a replacement is immediately started via `_create_process_for_shards`, but the old process object is never `join()`-ed. In production (spawn mode) each killed process becomes a zombie until the parent exits, and its `SpansBuffer` (with its Redis connection pool) is dropped from `self.buffers[process_index]` without being closed, leaking connections. Since restarts can happen repeatedly (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index), a consumer running for a long time can accumulate zombies and leaked Redis connections. The old process should be joined/cleaned up before or after starting the replacement.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is defined but never called anywhere; the restart path uses `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. Dead code invites confusion about which restart entrypoint to use and should be removed.

Per-process restart counters never reset, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer

`self.process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented and never reset, even after a process has been running healthily for a long time. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, a process that legitimately crashed 11 times over months of uptime (e.g. transient Redis outages) will cause `_ensure_processes_alive` to raise RuntimeError and take down the whole consumer. The counter should be reset once the replacement process has been observed healthy for some period. This was a pre-existing flaw for the single process, but multiplying the number of processes multiplies the probability of hitting it.

Tests only cover the threading (produce_to_pipe) path, never the multiprocessing path

Both consumer tests and test_flusher.py inject `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` and `partial` instead of the spawn-based `multiprocessing.Process` with `run_with_initialized_sentry`. None of the new multi-process behavior (process-per-shard spawn, argument pickling of per-shard SpansBuffer and shared Values, process restart in `_ensure_processes_alive`, join/terminate of real processes) is exercised. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts on dicts/counts, not that processes actually work. A regression in the spawn path (e.g. a pickling error in the new per-shard buffer or the new `shards` argument) would not be caught.

test_basic relies on a fixed 0.1s sleep for the flusher thread to observe the drift change

`test_basic` sets `current_drift` and then sleeps for 0.1s before `step.join()`, expecting the background flusher thread to have picked up the new drift and flushed the segment. There is no synchronization guaranteeing the thread reached the read of `current_drift` or completed the flush/produce within 100ms, so the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking can flake on slow/loaded CI. A poll-until-assertion loop (with timeout) would make this deterministic.

max_processes default of None means one process per shard, contradicting documented default of 1

`SpanFlusher.__init__` treats `max_processes=None` as `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, i.e. one process per shard. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option documents "Defaults to 1", and its click default is 1, so CLI-driven deployments get 1; but any other instantiation path that omits the argument (as all existing direct callers in tests and code do) silently spawns one process per assigned partition, each of which re-imports sentry/Django under spawn. This is a significant behavioral/memory difference depending on call path, and the docstring does not mention it. The default should be consistent (e.g. 1) or the behavior documented.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

When the derived English reference file cannot be opened (see separate finding), or the current file cannot be re-read, verifySafeHtml throws a plain RuntimeException. The surrounding verify() method only catches IOException and wraps it into a MojoExecutionException; an uncaught RuntimeException will propagate out of the mojo and abort the build with a stack trace rather than being added to the reported `messages` list. A verification tool should report the problem as a message (or wrap it in MojoExecutionException) so users get a readable diagnostic.

The English reference file is computed as file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties"). This only works for files under themes/src/main/resources-community whose English counterpart exists under themes/src/main/resources. For the JS themes (js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources-community and js/apps/account-ui/maven-resources-community) there is no sibling "maven-resources" directory containing the _en file in the community repository, so the English bundle cannot be loaded and the verifier throws a RuntimeException (see other finding) for every such file. Additionally, many community-only locales (e.g. messages_ca, messages_ka under resources-community) have no _en-independent counterpart issue but product resources may lack them too; any locale file whose English file does not exist at the rewritten path will crash the verification rather than being skipped or reported.

The choice format is correct only for the server-side FreeMarker themes (themes/src/main/resources...), where those files were updated consistently.

PropertyResourceBundle reads the file as ISO-8859-1 while the duplicate-key check uses UTF-8

verifyNoDuplicateKeys reads the file via Files.readString (UTF-8), but verifySafeHtml loads the same file with new PropertyResourceBundle(new FileInputStream(file)), and PropertyResourceBundle(Properties.load(InputStream)) decodes as ISO-8859-1. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` on the dataclass captures the timestamp when the module is imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created without an explicit `queued` value (e.g. via `from_integration`) will carry the same stale process-start time, defeating the field's apparent purpose of recording when the assignment change was queued. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

false_positives.candidate:
Task now passes `assignment_source` kwarg to provider `sync_assignee_outbound` implementations that were not updated

The task calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, but none of the concrete provider implementations (Jira, VSTS/GitHub, etc. — none are in this PR's changed files) declare an `assignment_source` parameter; the abstract method in `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` also still has signature `(external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs)`. For implementations that don't accept `**kwargs`, every outbound assignee sync for an issue-sync-enabled org will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`, breaking assignee sync entirely. The abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` signature (issues.py line ~397) was not updated to include the parameter, unlike `sync_status_outbound`.

`AssignmentSource.from_dict` returns `None` if the dict doesn't match the constructor (e.g. unknown keys from a stale producer, or a `queued` value of the wrong shape). When that happens in `sync_assignee_outbound` (task line 53-55), `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` returns True and the outbound sync proceeds — i.e. exactly the sync-loop this PR is meant to prevent is silently re-enabled for any malformed payload, with no logging to surface the parse failure. At minimum the failure should be logged.

Round-trip through dict does not preserve `queued` as a datetime

`to_dict()` serializes `queued` via `asdict` into a `datetime`, and `from_dict()` reconstructs it via `cls(**input_dict)`. Since dataclasses do not validate types, a payload where `queued` arrives as a string (e.g. after JSON serialization through Celery/Redis in some configurations) will be accepted silently, leaving `queued` as a `str`. Any future consumer relying on `queued` being a `datetime` (ordering, comparisons) will fail or behave incorrectly; there is no coercion or rejection in `from_dict`.

Inbound assignee sync ignores organization scoping for the assignment source check

In `sync_group_assignee_inbound`, `where_should_sync(integration, "inbound_assignee")` is called without an `organization_id`, so groups from all orgs with the integration are affected and assigned an `AssignmentSource` for the integration. That part is fine, but note the companion outbound path in `where_should_sync` (line 48) calls `should_sync(key)` with no sync source; this is the status path so it is currently correct, but if `AssignmentSource` propagation is later extended to status sync, this call site will need updating — worth confirming intent, since the `sync_status_outbound` abstract signature was changed in this PR to accept `assignment_source` yet no caller passes one, leaving dead API surface that is untested.

false_positives.candidate:
queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown require Python 3.13

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, but Queue.shutdown() and the ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs (3.11/3.12) this raises AttributeError at shutdown time (silently swallowed by the try/except, so workers are never told to stop and blocked worker threads never exit), and the `except queue.ShutDown` handlers would fail to even import-resolve at runtime. The graceful shutdown path is broken on supported Python versions; use a sentinel/Event-based approach instead.

Failed messages are marked completed and their offsets committed, silently dropping them

OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a `finally` block, so when result_processor raises, the offset is still considered complete and the commit loop will commit past it. Combined with the fact that ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows all exceptions (logs only), any message that fails processing (e.g. DB error, bad subscription data) is permanently lost with no retry and no DLQ — the offset is committed so it will never be redelivered. The existing test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts this drop-on-failure behavior. There should be a retry/DLQ path or the offset should remain outstanding (blocking commit) on failure so the message is redelivered.

Queues are unbounded — no backpressure despite docstring claim, risk of unbounded memory growth

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after enqueueing, so the arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as it can. If processing (DB-backed result handling) is slower than consumption, queues grow without limit, holding decoded messages and their Message objects in memory until OOM. The class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' guarantee is false as implemented. Either set maxsize and block/propagate backpressure in submit(), or bound total in-flight items.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain, losing final offset commits

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(), which is what drains the worker queues. Any messages processed after the last commit-loop iteration (up to the entire remaining queue contents at shutdown) will be processed but never committed. On restart/rebalance those messages are redelivered and reprocessed, which for non-idempotent result handling means duplicate side effects. The correct order is: stop accepting new work, drain queues, do a final get_committable_offsets/commit, then stop the commit thread.

join() unconditionally calls close(), causing double shutdown and ignoring its timeout

Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close() then join() on strategies. Here join() calls close() again: shutdown_event.set() and commit_thread.join() are harmless, but queue_pool.shutdown() runs a second time — each Queue.shutdown() (on 3.13) raises ValueError on already-shutdown queues (swallowed by the broad except, hiding errors), and worker.join() is called again. Additionally the `timeout` parameter of join() is accepted but never used, so a stuck worker blocks shutdown for the full 5s join regardless. join() should simply wait (using its timeout) for work to drain, not re-run shutdown.

Worker thread death permanently stalls offset commits for its queue

If an OrderedQueueWorker thread exits for any reason other than a clean shutdown — e.g. an exception raised by metrics.gauge or the sentry_sdk transaction wrapper inside the finally block, or a non-Exception BaseException from result_processor — the thread dies, but all offsets of items still sitting in its queue remain in OffsetTracker.outstanding forever. get_committable_offsets will never advance past the smallest such offset, so commits for that partition stop entirely, backpressure-free consumption continues enqueueing into a queue nobody reads, and memory grows until the process is killed. There is no liveness check or worker restart.

Arroyo Commit callable invoked from a background thread concurrently with the consumer thread

The commit loop thread calls the arroyo Commit function (which ends up calling consumer commit / interacting with consumer state) once per second, while the StreamProcessor's main thread concurrently polls the consumer and may itself commit or rebalance. Arroyo strategies normally call commit from the processing (main) thread; calling it from an unsynchronized background thread risks racing with the consumer during rebalances/shutdown and can produce errors or commits of stale offsets. This needs verification against arroyo's thread-safety contract, or the commit should be marshalled back to the strategy thread (e.g. via poll()).

test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to salted string hashing

The test asserts that 20 arbitrary group keys hashed with Python's builtin hash() (which is salted per process for str) land on exactly all 3 queues. With random salt it is possible (though unlikely) that fewer than 3 distinct indices are hit, making the test flaky across runs. Asserting `>= 2` or using fixed deterministic keys would be robust.

A sentry_sdk transaction is started for every single message in every worker

OrderedQueueWorker wraps each individual result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction. At production uptime-result volumes this creates and discards a transaction object per message (20 queues × full throughput), adding significant per-message overhead and, if any transaction sampling is enabled, flooding Sentry with events. The batched-parallel mode wraps batches, not items; this should be a span or sampled/omitted entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on Django querysets

The 'advanced features' branch does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django ORM querysets do not support negative indexing — slicing with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported in querysets`. The comment claims 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. Any request that reaches this branch (cursor with negative offset, `optimized_pagination=true`, privileged user) will produce a 500 instead of a page of results. Since cursors are client-supplied strings parsed by `Cursor.from_string`, a negative offset is trivially craftable, making this a denial-of-service on the endpoint.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the advanced-features negative-offset branch passes cursor.offset directly into queryset slicing as a negative start_offset. The candidate explains the resulting Django assertion failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now slices with unclamped negative offsets for prev cursors

The original code did `queryset[offset:stop]` and the new code does `start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, then slices. For non-prev cursors the `max(0, offset)` clamp prevents negative offsets, but for prev cursors the raw (possibly negative) offset is passed straight to queryset slicing. Combined with `Cursor.from_string` accepting any integer offset from the client, a malicious cursor such as `0:-5:1` on any endpoint using BasePaginator subclasses will hit Django's negative-slicing AssertionError (or, for list-backed paginators, silently return wrong rows). This changes behavior of every existing BasePaginator consumer, not just the new 'optimized' path, and is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in BasePaginator.get_result(): prev cursors use the raw offset as start_offset without clamping, allowing negative offsets to reach queryset slicing.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by datetime

The audit log endpoint sorts by `-datetime` and previously used `DateTimePaginator`, which converts datetimes to epoch-millis ints for cursor keys. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` is copied from the plain `Paginator` and does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` on the raw attribute; when the attribute is a `datetime`, `math.floor`/`int()` raise `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware...`/`type error`. So the optimized path crashes whenever it needs to compute an item key (any request with results). Additionally, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, whereas `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` converts the millis value back into a timezone-aware datetime for the SQL comparison — the optimized path would compare a float against a datetime column and break the query. The paginator is simply not usable for this endpoint's data type.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to a raw datetime when ordering by '-datetime', causing a TypeError. The additional cursor-conversion concern and imprecise exception wording do not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
zpopmin eviction silently drops buffered spans with no metric or cap configurability

The new eviction block pops `span_count - 1000` members off the set whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, permanently dropping those span payloads before they are ever flushed to the `buffered-spans` topic. The Python-side `max_segment_spans` guard (which skipped the segment and logged an error) was removed from `_load_segment_data` without replacement. The 1000 limit is hardcoded in Lua, is inconsistent with the Python `max_segment_spans = 1001` default, and there is no metric increment, log, or counter when eviction occurs — segments above 1000 spans will be silently truncated, making the data loss invisible in monitoring. Eviction also uses `zpopmin` (lowest end timestamp), meaning the oldest spans of a segment vanish, potentially including the root/segment span that later code (`is_segment` detection, redirect handling) depends on.

Redis structure changed from sets to sorted sets without migration handling

The script now calls `zcard`/`zunionstore` where it previously called `scard`/`sunionstore`. During a rolling deploy, old-version processes still write span payloads via `sadd`/`sunionstore` while new-version processes read them with `zcard`, so existing set-typed keys are invisible to the new logic (`zcard` on a set key returns a WRONGTYPE error in Redis, actually failing the EVALSHA call entirely). There is no migration or versioning strategy, so deploying this will produce errors/data loss for any in-flight traces buffered before the deploy. `buffer.py` also changed `sadd`→`zadd` and `sscan`→`zscan` symmetrically, but mixed-version operation during rollout is not handled.

Redirect traversal limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The redirect-following loop bound was cut from 10000 to 1000 with no explanation in the PR description and no constant shared with Python. The original comment noted the limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not join correctly; reducing to 1000 tightens that failure mode. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with `set_span_id` pointing at an intermediate node and the span is written to the wrong buffer key, splitting a segment — silently, since the returned `redirect_depth` metric is the only signal. If this reduction was intentional (e.g. to bound Redis script runtime), it should be documented and covered by a test; neither exists.

Undocumented, untested query-parameter-gated paginator switch on a control-silo endpoint

A new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter changes which paginator implementation and behavior (including negative-offset support) the audit log endpoint uses, but it is not documented in the API schema, not covered by any endpoint test, and the behavior difference is invisible to clients. The permission gate uses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` (owner/manager) or superuser, but audit logs are sensitive security data and the 'advanced' path offers no clear benefit while introducing the crash bugs above. This change is also entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (span buffer optimization), making it easy to miss in review.

paginate() may not forward enable_advanced_features to the paginator constructor

The call passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to `self.paginate(...)`. Whether this kwarg reaches `OptimizedCursorPaginator.__init__` depends on the endpoint base class's `paginate` implementation forwarding arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`; the standard `paginate` in sentry's API base constructs the paginator with a fixed set of arguments (queryset, order_by, etc.). If it does not forward the kwarg, this raises a TypeError (500) on every optimized request; if it does forward it, the default `enable_advanced_features=False` still enables the negative-offset branch only for this flag combination, which no test exercises. Either way there is no test covering this endpoint's new code path.

No tests for eviction, oversized segments, or the new sorted-set behavior

The core behavioral changes of this PR — segments exceeding 1000 spans being truncated via `zpopmin`, the removal of the `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data`, and the set→sorted-set conversion — have no test coverage. All existing tests use tiny traces (4-5 spans) with identical timestamps, so they cannot catch wrong sort scores, eviction of the wrong members, or eviction of the root span. A test that builds a segment of >1000 spans with distinct `end_timestamp_precise` values and asserts which spans survive is needed before this data-lossy change can be merged.

Pre-existing typo `order_b` means ASC conversion of descending order_by never applies

In `build_queryset`, the branch that converts an existing `-{key}` ordering back to ascending assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. While pre-existing, the new negative-offset/OptimizedCursorPaginator work sits directly on top of this path and the diff touches the surrounding function, so the bug now affects the new paginator too: a prev-cursor request on a queryset already ordered by `-datetime` will not have its ordering flipped to ASC, producing incorrectly ordered (and thus incorrectly paginated) results. Worth fixing while this code is being modified.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the call to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the closure variable `dataset` (the request's top-level dataset), not `scoped_dataset` (the dataset actually being queried). The dashboard-widget discover-split logic calls `_get_event_stats` with `discover` as the scoped dataset and an error-only query (`AND !event.type:transaction`), but the eligibility check still evaluates against the original dataset (often metrics-enhanced performance), which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, causing discover-backed queries such as dashboard splits to skip upsampling when the original dataset is metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
`_is_error_focused_query` uses naive substring match on raw query string

`if "event.type:error" in query` matches any occurrence of the substring, including negated filters like `!event.type:error` or `event.type:errorhabc`-style token prefixes, and it also ignores that the effective query can be rewritten by the caller (e.g. the endpoint's `(query) AND !event.type:transaction` split). A query that explicitly excludes errors (`!event.type:error`) will be treated as error-focused and have `count()` rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, which sums a `sample_weight` column that may not exist/apply, returning wrong counts or failing the query. The check should parse the actual filter AST rather than substring-match the raw string.

`upsampled_count` SnQL function only registered on the discover dataset

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True unconditionally when `dataset == errors`, and the endpoint then rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count`. But the `upsampled_count` function is only added to the discover dataset's `function_converter`. If the query actually runs against the errors dataset, the function is unregistered and the query builder will reject the column, breaking all errors-dataset stats queries for allowlisted projects. Either register the function on the errors dataset too, or never rewrite columns for that dataset.

`upsampled_count` declares result type "number" while `count()` is "integer"

The new function uses `default_result_type="number"` (a float) whereas the `count()` it replaces is `integer`. After the alias `as count`, API consumers (dashboards, alert thresholds, comparisons) receive floats like 10.0 instead of integers, and any downstream integer assertions/serialization of the `count` field changes shape. It should be `integer`, consistent with the alias it replaces (and with the `toInt64` wrapper already applied in the SnQL aggregate).

Cache key uses Python `hash()` and per-combination project sets, making invalidation impossible

The cache key is built from `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Beyond being needlessly opaque, the eligibility is cached per exact set of project IDs, so `invalidate_upsampling_cache(org, project_ids)` can only clear the one combination it is handed — removing a project from the allowlist leaves every other project-set combination stale for up to 60 seconds with no way to invalidate them. Additionally, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere in the codebase, so allowlist changes never proactively invalidate anything. If a project is removed from the allowlist, its events (which may now lack valid `sample_weight`) will continue to be summed via `upsampled_count()` for the TTL, producing wrong counts. A versioned key or a short shared per-org key would make invalidation tractable.

Tests mock `options` but not the eligibility cache, causing cross-test contamination

The new tests patch `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` but the real `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` also consults the shared Django cache keyed on org id + project ids with a 60s TTL. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches eligibility=True for that org/project set; subsequent tests in the same run that mock `options.get` to a partial or empty allowlist will still read the cached True and take the upsampling path, inverting the assertions (e.g. `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` and `test_error_upsampling_with_no_allowlisted_projects` expecting count==1 could see 10). The cache must be cleared or mocked per test, and the caching behavior itself is untested.

Accidental nested `sentry-repo` gitlink/submodule committed

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink pinning commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a. This appears to be an accidentally nested repository reference (likely from running tooling inside a checkout), not an intended submodule — there is no `.gitmodules` entry or description mention. It will confuse CI/checkout and should be removed from the commit.

`store_event` factory unconditionally copies `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` into top-level `sample_rate`

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` runs for every `store_event` call, mutating `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` whenever the context is present. This changes event-processing behavior for all existing tests that (even accidentally) include an `error_sampling` context, and it silently swallows all exceptions with bare `except Exception: pass`, masking real shape errors (e.g. `contexts` being None yields AttributeError that is hidden). If this is only needed for the upsampling tests, it should be opt-in (a `store_event` kwarg) rather than a global side effect.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key can collide with permission cache key (unescaped underscore concatenation)

userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by plain underscore concatenation: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Both userUID and name/parent are attacker-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores, so two distinct (user, action, name, parent) tuples can produce the same key (e.g. uid "a", action "x", name "b_c" vs uid "a", action "x", name "b", parent "c" with an underscore shift). Worse, the key shares the "<ns>.perm_" prefix space with userPermCacheKey(ns, userUID, action), so a denial entry for one user/action tuple can be read as another user's permission set (or vice versa) if components line up — in Check, permCache.Get is keyed by the same scheme and the denial cache shares the same underlying cache.Cache instance. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions (or hash/encode components) to make the keys unambiguous.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: unescaped underscore concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey can produce ambiguous keys and collisions between distinct component tuples, causing incorrect cache hits affecting permissions. Its additional cross-cache collision concern does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache reintroduces the exact bug this PR is meant to fix

The new negative cache caches a deny decision for shortCacheTTL (30s) keyed on (namespace, user, action, resource name, parent folder), and there is no invalidation when permissions or resources change. Scenario: a user requests a dashboard that does not yet exist / they have no permission for (Check returns deny and the entry is written at line 154). The user then creates that dashboard or folder (or an admin grants access). The very next Check for the same resource hits the denial entry at line 117 and is denied for up to 30 seconds, with no DB fallback. This is precisely the 'creator can't access the dashboard they just created' failure the PR description says it fixes — it is now bounded to ~30s instead of removed. Same for newly granted permissions: access is delayed by up to 30s. Consider invalidating the denial entry on writes, keying it more coarsely with shorter TTL, or not caching denials when the resource was simply absent from the scope map.

No test that a deny decision actually writes the denial cache entry

TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' case only verifies that a manually pre-populated permDenialCache entry causes a deny. There is no test asserting that after Check returns Allowed=false from a DB query, the service writes the denial entry (service.go:154) and that a subsequent Check for the same resource short-circuits without hitting the store. This is the core new behavior of the PR (negative caching) and its write path is untested; a regression that never writes the entry (making the whole feature a no-op) would pass the current suite.

Denial-cache hit misreported as a permission-cache hit in permissionCacheUsage metric

When the denial cache is hit, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit) even though the permission cache was not consulted. Additionally, when cached permissions exist but evaluate to deny, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" (line 137) despite the perm cache actually being hit. Both skew the cache-hit-rate metric in opposite directions, making it unusable for evaluating whether the caching changes are effective.

Deny path with cached permissions always re-queries the DB, defeating singleflight in common case

When a user has cached permissions that don't cover the requested resource (a very common deny case for legitimate users, e.g. dashboard they don't own), Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and performs a full DB permission query, and a denial entry is only written afterward. For users with genuinely no permission for the action at all, getIdentityPermissions returns an empty/stale-cached scope map which is re-fetched and re-set into permCache each time before checkPermission denies. The permCache is refreshed with identical data on every request for such users (singleflight only dedups concurrent, not sequential calls). Consider not re-setting permCache when the fetched map is identical, or caching 'no permissions for action' explicitly, to avoid write amplification on the hot deny path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError/TypeError on integrations whose metadata lacks 'sender'

GitHubInstallation.dispatch compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Integrations created through paths that don't set the sender metadata (e.g. created by the pipeline itself via build_integration, where `state.get("sender")` may be absent, or older integrations installed before sender tracking) have no `sender` key in metadata, so this raises KeyError (or TypeError if sender is not a dict), producing a 500 error page instead of the intended error response. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat missing sender explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the unguarded access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"], which raises a KeyError when sender metadata was not set during integration creation. The candidate's additional TypeError scenario does not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
User verification is skipped when the Integration does not exist yet

The authenticated-user-vs-installer check only executes in the branch where the Integration already exists but has no OrganizationIntegration (line 500-505). If the Integration.DoesNotExist branch is taken (line 481-482) — e.g. the installation webhook hasn't been processed yet, or the integration was deleted — the pipeline proceeds with `pipeline.next_step()` without any verification that the currently authenticated GitHub user is the one who installed the app, and the integration is then built with unverified state. false_positives.candidate:

Because the cache key only contains the requested locale, a cached fallback result will be reused even after the site's default_locale changes (or, on a multi-process deployment where the cache lives per process, results computed under an old default_locale persist until the cache is evicted or the process restarts). Users would see translations from the wrong locale until restart. The cache key should include the fallback chain (e.g. I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].join) or the cache must be cleared when default_locale changes.

FallbackLocaleList inherits from Hash but its `[]` ignores all hash state and always computes [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]. Background jobs, mailers, and any other entry point that sets I18n.locale (e.g. Discourse's job locale handling, I18n.locale = user locale) will use the fallback chain without the fallback locales being loaded into the backend. Because translate_accelerator forces explicit loading (load_translations ignores empty args) and only loads config.locale inside translate, lookups for the fallback locales (site default locale, or :en) will miss and silently return the next fallback — meaning users get English strings instead of the site-default-locale translations in emails and scheduled jobs. The ensure_loaded! should be invoked wherever I18n.locale is set outside controllers, or translate should load all fallback locales.
