false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
float: right on .small-action button is a no-op now that the parent is a flex container

`.small-action` was changed to `@include flexbox()`, but the `button { float: right; }` rule inside it was kept. Floats are ignored on flex items, so the button (e.g. the 'change owner' / moderation button rendered in small actions) will no longer be pushed to the right edge; it will sit inline after the description as an ordinary flex item. The rule should be replaced with a flex-based right alignment (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button), otherwise the small-action button placement regresses visually on topic pages.

Header right panel loses its right alignment on browsers using the legacy flexbox syntax

The old `float: right` on `.d-header .panel` was replaced with `margin-left: auto`. `margin-left: auto` for end-alignment only works in the modern flexbox model; the 2009 box model that the `flexbox()` mixin also emits (`display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`) does not honor auto margins — there you need `-webkit-box-pack: end` on the container. On any browser that only supports the old syntax (older Android/Safari that the prefixes were presumably added for), the login/sign-up panel will sit immediately after the title instead of being right-aligned, and since the floats were removed there is no fallback. Either add the box-pack fallback or keep a float-based fallback.

Removal of .title float leaves no layout for browsers without flexbox support

The diff deletes the `.d-header .contents .title { float: left; }` rule and replaces the layout entirely with the flexbox mixins on `.contents`. Browsers that support none of the five `display` variants emitted by `flexbox()` will fall back to block layout, where the title, extra-info and panel will each stack on their own line instead of laying out horizontally. If those browsers matter, a float fallback should be retained; otherwise the extra prefixed values serve no purpose.

order() mixin mixes 2009 and 2012 spec syntaxes that don't work together

The `order($val)` mixin emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` (2009 spec, integer-only, works only alongside `display: -webkit-box`) together with `-ms-flex-order`/`order`. In the corresponding layout files, `flexbox()` is applied to one element and `order(2)`/`order(3)` to different elements (.extra-info-wrapper, .panel), so within any single legacy engine only one of the pair of declarations applies and the reordering silently does nothing; also the 2009 engines require the group values to start at 1 (order 0 default vs. 2/3 here is fine, but the emitted 2009 declarations have no matching old-spec box on the sibling items). Practically this means visual order of the header contents differs between legacy and modern browsers; if legacy engines are not targeted, the 2009-era prefixes should be dropped from these mixins to avoid a false sense of compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking hidden TL0 profile data

The serializer defines `untrusted_attributes` to hide `website` (and bio, location, etc.) for TL0 users viewed anonymously, but the new `website_name` attribute was only added to the plain `attributes` list. As a result, when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true, the JSON omits `website` but still includes `website_name`, which now (when the website domain matches the instance domain) contains the full URL path. This leaks exactly the information the untrusted-attribute restriction is meant to hide, and it bypasses the existing spec at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11-15 which only checks the enumerated attribute list. `website_name` should be added to `untrusted_attributes` (and a test added).

website_name drops query string and fragment from the URL

When the website domain matches the instance domain, `website_name` is built as `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path`, discarding the query string and fragment. A profile website like `http://example.com/page?id=42` would be displayed as `example.com/page`, so the shown 'complete URL path' is wrong/incomplete for URLs with query parameters. Use `URI(website.to_s).request_uri` or `[path, query].compact.join('?')` instead.

Domain-matching logic misses websites on subdomains of the instance domain

The elsif branch only compares hosts when the label counts are equal and greater than 2, and the else branch only matches when the instance hostname ends with `.#{website_host}` (i.e. the website is a parent of the instance). A website on a subdomain of the instance domain, e.g. website `http://sub.forums.example.com/page` on instance `forums.example.com`, falls through to the else branch where the ends_with check fails, so only the bare host is shown even though it is under the same registrable domain and the PR's intent ('same domain') would suggest showing the full path. The three-way string-split comparison is also ad hoc: `a.b.example.com` vs `x.y.example.com` matches (showing full path) while `sub.forums.example.com` vs `forums.example.com` does not, which is inconsistent.

Scheme-less website URLs yield nil website_name while include_website_name stays true

`URI(website.to_s).host` is nil for values like `example.com/user` (no scheme), so `website_name` returns nil, yet `include_website_name` only checks `website.present?` and therefore still emits a `website_name: null` key. The old client-side `website.split("/")[2]` was equally limited, but if the profile website field accepts scheme-less input on any code path, the profile will render no website label at all where it previously showed the raw string in the link/title. Consider normalizing with a scheme before parsing and guarding inclusion on the computed value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Weak origin check on postMessage via substring match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any message whose origin appears anywhere in discourseUrl. E.g. with discourseUrl 'http://meta.discourse.org', a sender at 'http://meta.discourse.org.evil.com' passes the check (its origin string contains the discourseUrl as a substring) and can drive iframe.height with arbitrary values. The check should compare the parsed origin of discourseUrl to e.origin with strict equality.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify insufficient postMessage origin validation using indexOf and recommend exact origin matching. The candidate's example reverses the substring direction and would not pass the quoted check, but it still identifies the same underlying security issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls methods on i.content without checking presence. Many RSS feeds provide only a description/summary and no content element (simple-rss returns nil for missing tags), so the scheduled job will raise NoMethodError on nil. With `sidekiq_options retry: false` the exception is swallowed and, more importantly, it aborts processing of the remaining feed items in the same run, so topics after the offending item are never imported until the next hour. Guard with `i.content || i.description` or a nil check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: calling scrub on a potentially nil i.content when RSS items lack content, and recommend falling back to i.description to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer header injected unescaped into inline JavaScript

The layout embeds `'<%= request.referer %>'` directly inside a <script> block. The referer is an attacker-controlled HTTP header; ensure_embeddable only checks that URI(referer).host equals the configured embeddable_host, so a referer such as `http://<embeddable_host>/';alert(1);//` passes the host check and breaks out of the JS string literal (and `</script>` sequences break out of the script tag entirely), executing arbitrary script in the Discourse iframe origin. The value must be JSON/JS-escaped (e.g. `json_escape`/to_json) and ideally validated as a full origin before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same XSS vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated into inline JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing attacker-controlled header content to execute arbitrary scripts.

false_positives.candidate:
RSS feed content is stored and rendered as raw HTML without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method: raw_html, which makes Post#cook return raw unchanged (app/models/post.rb line 133). When called from the PollFeed path (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35-36), `contents` is the raw feed item content with only CGI.unescapeHTML applied — no HTML sanitization occurs. The embed view (app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19) then renders these posts with `raw post.cooked`. Any <script>, inline event handlers, or other malicious markup in the external feed is stored verbatim and executed in the Discourse origin for every visitor of the embedded page, allowing a compromised or malicious feed to hijack Discourse sessions/perform CSRF. The import_remote path limits tags/attributes via readability, but the feed path has no such filtering; contents should be sanitized (e.g. via Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

feed_key is dead code; no conditional-fetch deduplication is implemented

The `feed_key` method (used nowhere) and its 'feed-modified:' redis key suggest the intent was to skip polling when the feed has not changed (e.g. via Last-Modified/ETag), but poll_feed unconditionally re-opens the feed URL and re-processes every item every hour. Every existing embed's content is re-fetched/recomputed and each unchanged item still goes through a TopicEmbed lookup and SHA1 comparison; if content SHA matches it is skipped only after the DB read. Either remove the dead method or wire it up to store/compare the feed's modified time so polling is skipped when unchanged.

setnx followed by separate expire is not atomic

retrieved_recently? uses $redis.setnx and then a separate $redis.expire. If the process dies (or redis restarts) between the two calls, the key 'retrieved:<url>' exists with no TTL and permanently blocks retrieval for that embed URL until manual redis intervention. Use a single SET key value EX 60 NX (or setex-style) operation so the TTL is set atomically with the key creation.

Update path crashes if the embedded post has been deleted

On re-import of an existing embed, `post = embed.post` is used without a nil check before `PostRevisor.new(post)` and `embed.update_column`. If the topic's post was deleted (or post_id points to a removed record — the association has no dependent handling and nothing destroys the TopicEmbed when its post is destroyed), the poll job will raise NoMethodError on nil every run for that URL. Guard for a missing post (and consider destroying the TopicEmbed alongside the post).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of self.downsize; first (width/height) form is dead code

The class now defines `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and then redefines `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. Ruby silently discards the first definition (with a 'method redefined' warning in some modes), and both have the same arity so callers passing width and height as separate integers will now hit the second definition and produce a broken dimension string like "640x480" vs "1024-768"-style concatenation issues... concretely, a caller invoking downsize(from, to, 100, 75) now gets dimensions "100" passed to ImageMagick (75 is bound to opts), producing wrong output rather than an error. The two-integer variant should be removed entirely or the definitions merged, not left as shadowed duplicate definitions.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same duplicate downsize definition and explains that the dimensions-string version overrides the separate width/height version, breaking existing callers. Minor inaccuracies about arity and downstream behavior do not change the underlying issue identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client-side limit ignores SiteSetting max image/attachment sizes

The client-side upload validation previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'] (i.e. max_image_size_kb / max_attachment_size_kb) but now hardcodes 10MB. This breaks validation in both directions: on sites where the admin set a lower limit (e.g. 4MB), oversized files pass the client check and only fail on the server with a confusing generic error; and the hardcoded 10MB cap cannot be raised by admins. The same hardcode in the 413 handler (line 246) shows users a wrong maximum size in the error message. The stated goal of the PR (allow large images that the server will downsize) is undermined because the client still blocks any image over 10MB and, worse, blocks images over the (possibly small) configured limit that the new server-side downsizing was meant to accept — the client check should be relaxed or removed for images, not fixed at 10MB.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10MB limit ignoring per-type Discourse.SiteSettings, causing client/server limit divergence and an incorrect maximum-size message in the 413 handler.

false_positives.candidate:
In-place downsize: convert is run with input and output as the same file path

OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...) executes ImageMagick's `convert /tmp/xxx /tmp/xxx`, i.e. the source and destination are the same path. ImageMagick reads the input lazily and can truncate/corrupt the file while writing, or fail outright, depending on format and buffering. The result can be a corrupted or zero-byte upload. The downsized output should be written to a separate temp file and then replace the original.

Animated GIFs lose animation and animated path is never selected for uploads

The animated-image branch in OptimizedImage.optimize is chosen only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but `tempfile.path` for an uploaded file is a Tempfile path with no .gif extension (e.g. /tmp/d discourse-upload...). So animated GIFs always go through `convert #{from}[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame, silently destroying animation. Additionally, `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is passed, but the actual check inside optimize tests the file path's extension, not the flag, so the setting has no effect here. Files with no recognizable animation possible (corrupt images) will also make `convert` fail repeatedly (see next finding).

Downsize loop ignores failures and still submits the oversized file

The while loop decrements `attempt` but never checks the return value of OptimizedImage.downsize, which returns false when convert fails (corrupt image, missing ImageMagick, etc.). On failure the file size never changes, so the loop pointlessly shells out 5 times and then passes the still-oversized file to Upload.create_for, which will reject it with a generic error. The loop should break out and fail fast (or surface a clear error) when downsize returns false.

API URL download cap hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

FileHelper.download for API-provided URLs now uses a fixed 10.megabytes cap instead of SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes. On sites where max_image_size_kb (or max_attachment_size_kb) is configured above 10MB, valid API uploads are now truncated/fail at 10MB with no way to configure it; below 10MB, non-image downloads are no longer bounded by the image setting at all. The cap should be derived from the relevant setting (e.g. [max_image_size_kb, max_attachment_size_kb].max) rather than hardcoded.

Downsized image keeps original filename but stored sha/filesize mismatch metadata assumptions

After downsizing, the upload is created with the original `filename` and the new (smaller) tempfile.size, but the content no longer matches the file the user chose; more importantly, uploads of type where FileHelper.is_image? matches by extension (e.g. .svg) will run ImageMagick `convert` on an SVG with "80%" geometry, which either rasterizes the SVG (destroying its vector nature) or fails. SVGs should be excluded from the downsize path the same way OptimizedImage.create_for special-cases .svg.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate: GET /unsubscribe toggles state and crashes when no TopicUser record exists The unsubscribe action performs a state-changing toggle on a plain GET request. Two concrete problems: (1) `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` returns nil when the logged-in user has no topic_users row for that topic (e.g. they received the email via a mention/watch category without ever visiting, or the row was cleaned up); `tu.notification_level` on the next line then raises NoMethodError, producing a 500 instead of a graceful response. It should use TopicUser.change or handle the nil case. (2) Because the toggle is a side effect of a GET, simply refreshing or re-visiting the emailed link flips the user back and forth between muted and regular, and any third-party page can trigger the state change for a logged-in user via an /link (CSRF via GET). The mutation should be a POST/PUT (or done through the Ember route with an explicit action), not performed on every GET.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same nil-reference bug: TopicUser.find_by can return nil when no record exists, and accessing tu.notification_level then raises NoMethodError. The additional GET-related concerns do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Direct tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

The unsubscribe action sets notification_level directly on the TopicUser AR object and calls save!, instead of using TopicUser.change. TopicUser.change is the canonical path that also stamps notifications_changed_at, notifications_reason_id, publishes the MessageBus notification_level_change event to the user's open tabs, and handles record creation races. Saving directly leaves notifications_changed_at/reason stale and open clients won't see the level change until reload.

unsubscribe_link now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email that sets add_unsubscribe_link without it

The rewritten `unsubscribe_link` locale string now interpolates both %{user_preferences_url} and %{unsubscribe_url}. Email::MessageBuilder#body and #html_part call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args) whenever @opts[:add_unsubscribe_link] is true, but unsubscribe_url is only supplied by UserNotifications#send_notification_email. Any other builder invocation with add_unsubscribe_link: true and no :unsubscribe_url option (other mailers, plugins, or future call sites — and the old spec case before it was patched in this same PR) will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument (or emit a broken literal `%{unsubscribe_url}` link) when building the email. The per-topic sentence should be a separate locale key used only when the URL is present.

No request specs for the unsubscribe controller action or route

The PR adds a new authenticated, state-mutating controller action (topics#unsubscribe) plus two new routes, but includes no request/controller specs covering: the redirect when the slug is missing/mismatched, the toggle behavior at each starting notification level, the nil-TopicUser case, access control for topics the user cannot see, and the logged-out redirect. The only test touched is the message_builder spec, so the most fragile new code (the toggling GET) ships untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' syntax is macOS-only and fails on Linux

The script uses `sed -i '' -E "..." "$ENV_FILE"`. On GNU/Linux sed, `-i ''` is interpreted as an empty file operand and the command fails, so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated on Linux dev machines. Also the relative `ENV_FILE="../.env"` depends on the caller's cwd. Use a portable check (e.g. `sed -i.bak`) or detect the platform.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same portability bug: macOS-style `sed -i ''` fails on GNU/Linux. The additional concern about the relative path does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure thrown as generic Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential isn't found/owned, the handler throws a plain `Error('Credential not found or access denied')`, which tRPC surfaces as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) with the message leaking to the client. Cal.com's convention is to throw `TRPCError({ code: 'UNAUTHORIZED' | 'NOT_FOUND' })` so clients get correct status codes and no server error noise/alerting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: throwing a generic Error for authentication or authorization failure causes tRPC to return HTTP 500 instead of a structured TRPCError with an appropriate status code. The suggested codes differ, but the underlying bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp hardcoded to en-US and ignores user locale

The cache 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` instead of using the user's locale from `useLocale()`. All non-US users will see US-formatted dates (MM/DD/YYYY, 12-hour clock), inconsistent with the rest of the localized UI.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: date formatting hardcodes the en-US locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, resulting in inappropriate date representations for other locales.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache ownership check fails for delegated credentials

The handler authorizes the request with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. Delegation credentials often have `userId: null` (or an in-memory/negative id), so a user whose Google calendar is connected via a DelegationCredential will always get 'Credential not found or access denied' even though the UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) shows the 'Delete cached data' action for those credentials (hasCache is true when delegationCredentialId is set and canDisconnect is false). The user will always see 'Error deleting cache'. The check needs to account for delegated-to credentials the user has access to, or the UI must hide the delete action for them.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

After successfully deleting the cache via `trpc.viewer.calendars.deleteCache`, the component only calls `onSuccess?.()`. Unlike the disconnect mutation (which invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in onSettled), the delete-cache path never invalidates the `connectedCalendars` query. In the web wrapper `onChanged` is often undefined, so the UI will keep showing the old 'Cache Status / Last updated' timestamp (and the delete option) until an unrelated refetch happens, making the user think deletion didn't work.

Nested interactive elements / non-interactive DropdownMenuItem

`DropdownItem` (renders a `<button>`) is nested inside `DropdownMenuItem`, which itself renders a menu item element — this produces invalid nested interactive DOM and can break keyboard navigation and screen readers. The cache-status block is also rendered as a selectable menu item (line 84) that does nothing when clicked/activated, which is confusing for keyboard users; it should be a non-interactive label.

Deleting the cache does not repopulate it while webhooks remain active

`deleteCacheHandler` deletes all CalendarCache rows for the credential but leaves the Google webhook channel subscriptions intact and never triggers `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`. The cache is only repopulated on webhook events (which only fire on actual calendar changes) or the unwatch flow. For organizations relying on the calendar-cache feature, this means after deletion every availability check falls back to live Google freebusy API calls indefinitely until some calendar change occurs, defeating the purpose of the cache and risking Google API quota exhaustion. Deletion should trigger a re-fetch (as `unwatchCalendar` does with `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`).

updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data object is opaque and fragile

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` relies on Prisma's implicit `@updatedAt` bump when `data` is empty to work at all. This is undocumented/fragile behavior (some Prisma versions reject empty update data), updates rows even when the preceding cache writes failed, and communicates no intent. It also clobbers nothing but bumps `updatedAt` for all selected calendars of the credential, which the PR description itself flags as unused by the frontend — either give it an explicit data payload or remove the call until the field is consumed.

No tests for new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds or deleteCache handler

The PR adds a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, including the groupBy/_max mapping and null handling), a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), and new enrichment logic in `connectedCalendarsHandler`, but includes no unit or e2e tests for any of them. In particular the credential-ownership check and the empty-credentialIds edge case are untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check compares UTC slot minutes against organizer-timezone working hours

In the new working-hours validation inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, `slotStartTime` is a UTC dayjs, so `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` yields minutes since midnight UTC. But `workingHour.startTime/endTime` (from `getUserAvailability` / `getAggregateWorkingHours`) are minutes since midnight in the organizer's timezone. For any organizer not in UTC (e.g. Asia/Kolkata in the test data, working hours 09:30–18:00 local), the comparison `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` uses the wrong clock, wrongly marking valid in-hours slots as unavailable or letting out-of-hours slots through. Additionally, `const end` is computed identically to `const start` (both from `slotStartTime`), so the `end > workingHour.endTime` condition never tests the slot's end time — the event length is not accounted for at all.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate primarily discusses a timezone mismatch, it explicitly identifies that end is computed from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, matching the golden issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object-identity comparison makes the unavailability-override check dead code

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the check `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false regardless of the underlying times. The intent (per the surrounding logic) was to detect a zero-length override, i.e. an override marking the whole day unavailable (start === end). Such 'blocked day' overrides will not be recognized by this branch; instead they fall through to the subsequent `slotEndTime.isBefore(...)` checks, which for an empty range will mark every slot as outside the override and the day will incorrectly become unavailable (or available depending on order) — in any case the special-cased behavior can never trigger and is dead code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === to compare newly created dayjs objects compares references rather than date values, so the condition always evaluates to false. The candidate's additional discussion of consequences does not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check entirely

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, once a slot is found to be on a day with a date override and inside the override window, the function returns `true` immediately (`if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }`) without ever evaluating the `busy` array. This means that for fixed hosts (the primary path this PR adds, where `checkIfIsAvailable` is the only busy-time filter), any existing booking or calendar busy time that falls inside a date-override window will be reported as available. The attendee can be shown (and attempt to book) a slot where the host already has a meeting. The override should restrict the time window, not bypass conflict checking.

Date overrides that cross midnight in the invitee timezone are silently dropped

The new override computation converts the override start/end to minutes since midnight in the invitee timezone (`dayjs(...).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`). `hour()` wraps at 24, so an override such as 23:00–01:00 (invitee time) produces `startTime: 1380, endTime: 60`. `buildSlots` then skips this timeframe via the `if (start >= end) continue;` guard, so the override disappears entirely instead of splitting into two ranges. The previous code had the same wrap problem, but this rewrite was the opportunity to fix it; users with overnight overrides will see their normal working hours applied (or no availability) instead of the override.

Override-day matching compares organizer-local date against UTC slot date

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares the organizer-local calendar date of the override start with the UTC calendar date of the slot. For organizers in non-UTC timezones, slots in the first hours of a UTC day (or last hours) belong to a different local day, so the override-day detection is off by one day for those slots. Slots just after midnight UTC on the override day will not be treated as override-day slots (and vice versa), producing wrong availability at day boundaries.

No test for the fixed-host date override in a round-robin team event

The PR's headline fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected in round-robin events (issue #8207), but the added test only covers a single-user event with a date override and a different invitee timezone. There is no test with a ROUND_ROBIN event containing an `isFixed` host with a date override plus a non-fixed host, so the main code path added in `getSchedule` (`fixedHosts.every(...)` with date overrides) and the buggy busy-time bypass it introduces are not exercised by any test.

DST offset computed once from override start may be wrong for override end

The offset applied to the override is derived from a single instant (`override.start`): `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()`. If the override range spans a DST transition (possible for multi-hour or multi-day overrides), the end time is shifted by the start instant's offset, misplacing the end of the availability window by the DST delta. The offset should be evaluated at the respective instant for both start and end.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount increment uses stale in-memory value

The update writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` based on the value read when the batch was queried, rather than an atomic `increment: { retryCount: 1 }`. If the cron job runs concurrently (overlapping invocations or a manual trigger while the scheduled run is in progress), increments can be lost, so a reminder can fail more than twice before being deleted. Use `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that incrementing retryCount from a stale in-memory value can lose updates during concurrent executions and recommend Prisma's atomic increment to prevent the race condition.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS reminders

The `deleteMany` uses `OR: [{method: SMS, scheduledDate lte now}, {retryCount > 1}]`. The second branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` and no `scheduled`/`scheduledDate` condition, so any WorkflowReminder row of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) whose retryCount exceeds 1 will be deleted by this SMS cron job. Today only this file increments retryCount, but the column is on the shared WorkflowReminder model and any other code path (or a future email/whatsapp retry implementation) that increments it will have its reminders silently destroyed by the SMS scheduler. The retryCount condition should be conjoined with `method: SMS` (and ideally `scheduled: false`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion branch, which causes the SMS scheduler to delete non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders skipped due to empty message or missing sendTo never increment retryCount

The retryCount increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)`. When `sendTo` is null/empty (e.g. booking has no smsReminderNumber and step action is not SMS_NUMBER) or the computed message is empty, neither the success nor the failure branch runs, so retryCount stays 0 and the reminder is re-fetched and re-skipped on every cron run until scheduledDate passes — exactly the 'kept scheduling until date is reached' behavior this PR claims to fix. These reminders should either be deleted or have retryCount incremented so they are purged.

Exhausted reminders are silently deleted with no audit or notification

When a reminder exceeds the retry limit it is hard-deleted from the WorkflowReminder table. There is no log, no record of which booking/step failed, and no signal to the workflow owner, so users silently stop receiving SMS reminders (e.g. invalid phone numbers) with no way to diagnose it. Consider logging the deleted reminder ids or soft-cancelling (setting `cancelled`) instead of deleting, and/or notifying the workflow owner.

Public findMany() method removed, breaking existing callers

The refactor deletes the class's `findMany()` method, which was the main query entry point that took Prisma `BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs` and returned bookings. It is replaced only by `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any existing code that constructs `InsightsBookingService` and calls `service.findMany({ select, where, ... })` will now fail to compile or throw at runtime. The PR contains no changes to callers, so unless all call sites were already migrated in a prior PR, this is a breaking API change. The PR description also does not mention any caller migration.

Passing JS arrays to `= ANY(...)` may fail depending on Prisma driver serialization

In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 164/168) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 201), plain JavaScript arrays are interpolated into `Prisma.sql` and used as `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})`. Depending on the Prisma engine/driver version, raw query parameters that are JS arrays are not always serialized as PostgreSQL array types, which can produce errors like "op ANY/ALL (array) requires array on right side" or unexpected type coercion for the `teamIds` (int) case. The idiomatic safe form is `${Prisma.join(teamIds)}` inside the parentheses or an explicit `::int[]` cast. Since the author explicitly states the integration tests were never run ("I encountered test runner configuration issues"), this serialization risk is unverified and the query construction should be confirmed to actually execute against a real database before merging.

Integration tests were never executed; author flags manual verification as required

The PR description states the test runner had configuration issues during development and asks a human to "Run integration tests manually" because the author could not verify them. The entire PR's purpose is to make these tests pass against the new raw-SQL implementation, yet there is no evidence they were run. Merging unexecuted tests for authorization-critical SQL (org/team scoping, owner/admin checks) risks shipping broken queries that either fail at runtime or, worse, produce conditions that leak or wrongly restrict data. The tests must be executed and passing in CI before merge.

Caching behavior tests were deleted without replacement

The old test suite had a dedicated "Caching" describe block asserting that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return identical (cached) results on repeated calls. The refactor keeps the caching fields (`cachedAuthConditions`, `cachedFilterConditions`) and logic but the tests for it were removed entirely. Since the cache field types changed (from Prisma where-input objects to `Prisma.Sql`), a regression here (e.g., `Prisma.Sql` identity checks failing, or an always-truthy `1=0` fragment being treated as 'already computed') would go undetected.

Final integration test asserts exact result set and depends on denormalized-table cleanup

The `getBaseConditions` test runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ${baseConditions}` and asserts the result is exactly one row (`[...toEqual([{ id: userBooking.id }])]`). Because `createTestData` also creates a booking tied to a team event type, and other tests/users may leave residual rows, any leftover denormalized row matching the same `userId`/`teamId IS NULL`/`eventTypeId` conditions will make this assertion fail or, conversely, hide bugs. The cleanup deletes the `Booking` rows but there is no explicit cleanup of `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` rows; if that table is not cascade-deleted with bookings, stale rows from prior test runs will accumulate and break the strict `toEqual`. An assertion on membership (`results.some(r => r.id === userBooking.id)` / length filtering) or explicit denormalized-row cleanup would be more robust.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Placeholder refresh_token overwrites real refresh tokens in the database

When the parsed response lacks a refresh_token (which is the normal case for the self-hoster sync endpoint that only returns access token and expiry), the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers (Zoom, Webex, Google, Office365, Zoho) then persist this parsed object as the credential key. The real refresh token is permanently replaced by the literal string "refresh_token", so the next refresh attempt (and any fallback that disables sync) will fail with invalid_grant and the credential becomes unrecoverable. The old refresh_token must be merged in by the caller before saving, not defaulted to a bogus placeholder.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", resulting in an invalid token and subsequent refresh/authentication failures. The candidate adds details about persistence without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Computed zod schema keys are invalid and will reject all responses when credential sync is enabled

The schema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. `z.string().toString()` does not produce a real property name (it stringifies the ZodString object, e.g. "[object Object]"), so the resulting schema requires a numeric property literally named e.g. "[object Object]" and a second garbage key. Any real OAuth token response (which has keys like `expires_in`, `expiry_date`) will fail `safeParse`, so whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, every token refresh for Google, Office 365, Zoom and Salesforce will throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" and those integrations break. The intended behavior (accept any numeric expiry property and allow extra fields) needs `.passthrough()` and a union/optional expiry field, not computed keys.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: computed keys derived from Zod schemas in minimumTokenResponseSchema are invalid and cause refresh-token response validation to fail at runtime. The candidate adds details about the resulting property names and affected integrations, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync endpoint response shape is incompatible with all callers

When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response of CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, but every call site was written against the original provider's response type: Google reads `res?.data` (undefined on a fetch Response, so `token.access_token`/`expiry_date` become undefined and undefined is persisted to the credential), Hubspot expects the SDK's camelCase `HubspotToken` object, Lark passes the response to `handleLarkError` which requires Lark's `{code:0, data:{...}}` envelope, and Office365-video/Zoom/Webex/Zoho pass it to handlers expecting axios `response.data`. There is no contract (documented or validated) for the sync endpoint's response body, and the code never parses it before use, so token refresh is broken or corrupts credentials for every integration when the feature is turned on.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same sync-enabled return-type mismatch: the refresh helper returns a raw fetch Response, while callers expect provider-specific token objects or response envelopes. The candidate adds more affected integrations but describes the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync endpoint response shape is incompatible with all callers

When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response of CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, but every call site was written against the original provider's response type: Google reads `res?.data` (undefined on a fetch Response, so `token.access_token`/`expiry_date` become undefined and undefined is persisted to the credential), Hubspot expects the SDK's camelCase `HubspotToken` object, Lark passes the response to `handleLarkError` which requires Lark's `{code:0, data:{...}}` envelope, and Office365-video/Zoom/Webex/Zoho pass it to handlers expecting axios `response.data`. There is no contract (documented or validated) for the sync endpoint's response body, and the code never parses it before use, so token refresh is broken or corrupts credentials for every integration when the feature is turned on.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the inconsistent return shape of refreshOAuthTokens: the sync path returns a raw fetch Response, while callers expect provider-specific token data such as res.data. The candidate describes the same underlying bug, although it inaccurately describes Google's consequence as persisting undefined rather than throwing when accessing token.access_token.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
credentialId passed to refreshOAuthTokens instead of userId

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's id where the function expects the user's id (`calcomUserId`). When credential sync is enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint receives the credential id as `calcomUserId`, so it cannot resolve the right user and the token refresh will fail or return the wrong user's tokens. All other call sites pass `credential.userId`; this should too.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing credentialId instead of userId to refreshOAuthTokens causes incorrect user lookups and breaks credential syncing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Response success checked via response.statusText instead of response.ok

`if (response.statusText !== "OK")` relies on the human-readable reason phrase, which is not guaranteed to be "OK" for 200 responses across HTTP/2 (where reason phrases don't exist) or proxies. Use `response.ok` / `response.status === 200`, otherwise valid refreshes may be rejected or errors misclassified.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: checking response.statusText instead of response.ok for OAuth refresh success can incorrectly reject successful responses and cause authentication problems.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refreshed Salesforce access token saved to DB but not used for the connection

In `getClient`, the newly fetched token is validated and persisted via `prisma.credential.update`, but the returned `jsforce.Connection` is still constructed with the stale `credentialKey.access_token` (line 106). The first API call after refresh therefore uses the expired token and fails; the refreshed token only takes effect the next time the service is constructed. Use `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` (and the refreshed instance_url) when building the connection.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that jsforce.Connection uses stale credential values after a token refresh instead of the refreshed access token and instance URL, potentially causing authentication failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No HTTP method check and unhandled zod/JSON.parse errors cause 500s

The handler runs for any HTTP method (GET, DELETE, etc.) and does not guard `req.method === "POST"`. Additionally `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on malformed ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext; neither is caught, so invalid requests produce unhandled 500 errors with stack traces instead of 400s. Wrap parsing in safeParse, return 400 on failure, and restrict the handler to POST.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same issue: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws on invalid payloads without error handling, producing 500 responses instead of 400s. The additional HTTP method and JSON parsing concerns do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
symmetricDecrypt called with empty-key fallback; unvalidated decrypted payload written to credential key

`symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` silently falls back to an empty key. If the env var is unset (e.g. only CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is configured), decryption either fails obscurely or, depending on symmetricDecrypt's behavior with an empty key, may succeed incorrectly. More importantly, the decrypted value is `JSON.parse`d and written directly as the credential `key` with no schema validation — any JSON of any shape is accepted and persisted, so a compromised/misbehaving sender can store arbitrary credential payloads that will later crash app services when they try to use them. Validate against the app's expected credential schema before persisting, and fail loudly if the encryption key is missing.

Credential lookup ignores type and can overwrite team credentials

`prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` matches any credential for the user with that appId, including team-owned or differently-typed credentials (a user can legitimately have multiple credentials for the same app, e.g. google_calendar plus google_video share client ids across app slugs, and apps like office365 expose both calendar and video types). The webhook update will then overwrite whichever credential `findFirst` happens to return (no orderBy, so nondeterministic), potentially clobbering a team credential or the wrong app-type credential. Scope the lookup by `type: appMetadata.type` (and exclude team credentials) as done on create.

Outbound token sync request is unauthenticated and has no timeout

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no authentication (no webhook secret or signature), so the receiving self-hoster endpoint cannot verify the request actually came from its Cal.com instance, and anyone who can reach the endpoint can request access tokens for arbitrary users. There is also no timeout or non-200 handling — a slow or failing endpoint will hang every booking that triggers a token refresh. Attach the CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header and check the response status before returning.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED depends on CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT too, misleading gating

The flag is true whenever CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY are set, even if CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is empty. In that configuration the webhook is enabled but every refresh call site takes the normal path (each also checks the endpoint separately), which is arguably intended — but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` switches to the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` based on both flag and endpoint while `refreshOAuthTokens` uses the same pair of conditions evaluated at different times, making the behavior inconsistent and hard to reason about. Consolidate the enablement condition (flag + endpoint) into one shared constant so webhook receipt and refresh-path behavior cannot diverge.

Webhook secret compared with strict equality (not timing-safe)

The CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header is compared using `!==`, which is not constant-time. Use a timing-safe comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on digested values) for secret verification, as is standard for webhook endpoints, to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte to an attacker who can make repeated requests.

Missing Content-Type header on the sync POST request

The fetch to the credential sync endpoint sends a `URLSearchParams` body but no `Content-Type` header. While fetch infers `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for URLSearchParams in modern runtimes, the endpoint contract is undocumented and some servers/parsers require the explicit header; a request that the receiving endpoint can't parse will silently break token refresh. Set `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" }` and document the expected request/response contract for self-hosters.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Try/catch around reminder cancellation is ineffective; promises are fire-and-forget and cancellation can be lost

In the reschedule path, deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async functions invoked inside a synchronous forEach without await. The surrounding try/catch can never catch anything since no promise is awaited; if the serverless function returns and the process is frozen/terminated before the pending DB updates or SendGrid/Twilio calls complete, the old booking's reminders remain active and are sent for the cancelled slot. The calls should be awaited (e.g. Promise.all over the mapped promises).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: asynchronous reminder deletion functions are invoked without await inside forEach loops, allowing cancellation to remain incomplete and old reminders to stay active. It focuses on rescheduling rather than all affected paths, but this is the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path cancels at SendGrid but leaves the DB row as scheduled=true with a live referenceId

When immediateDelete is set (workflow deletion, deleted/edited steps, reschedule in handleNewBooking), the function POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns without deleting or flagging the WorkflowReminder row. The row remains scheduled=true with its referenceId until the CRON's `deleteMany where scheduledDate <= now` cleanup runs (which only happens for email reminders whose date has passed). Until then, any other code that iterates a booking's or workflow's reminders (e.g. a subsequent reschedule, or workflows.update's edited-step path) will try to cancel the same batch again and can hit errors, and the stale rows misrepresent state. The row should be deleted (or at least marked cancelled) in this branch too.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the immediateDelete branch cancels the SendGrid email but leaves the WorkflowReminder database record unchanged, creating stale/orphaned entries. The candidate omits the missing SendGrid DELETE call, but clearly matches the core underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Cron re-schedules and sends emails for reminders already marked cancelled

The query that finds unscheduled email reminders to schedule (around line 80) filters only on method=EMAIL, scheduled=false and scheduledDate <= now+72h, but does not exclude reminders with cancelled=true. When a booking is cancelled, deleteScheduledEmailReminder only sets cancelled=true on the DB row; if the reminder was not yet scheduled (referenceId null, scheduledDate >72h out at booking time), the row stays in the DB with cancelled=true and scheduled=false. The CRON job will then pick it up in the 'unscheduledReminders' query and schedule/send the email anyway — exactly the bug this PR claims to fix. The where clause needs `cancelled: false` (or cancelled: null), and cancelled-but-unscheduled rows should be deleted.

Cancel query includes SMS reminders and reminders without a referenceId, and one SendGrid error aborts all cancellations

The remindersToCancel query (line 44) has no method filter, so cancelled SMS reminders (whose referenceId is a Twilio SID) are POSTed to SendGrid's /v3/user/scheduled_sends endpoint, which will fail. Likewise, cancelled reminders with referenceId=null (never scheduled) produce a batch_id of null and SendGrid returns an error. Because the loop `await client.request(...)` throws on the first failure, execution jumps to the catch block, so the accumulated workflowReminder.delete() promises collected so far are never executed and all remaining reminders in the list are not cancelled that run. Filter on method=EMAIL and referenceId not null, and handle per-reminder errors instead of aborting the batch.

Reminder cancellation on booking cancel is fire-and-forget and unawaited

The forEach at line 485 calls async deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder without awaiting them. If the request handler completes (or the serverless invocation ends) before those promises resolve, the `cancelled: true` flag is never written and the scheduled email/SMS is still sent for the cancelled booking. These calls set the DB state that the CRON job depends on, so they must be awaited before responding.

Cron schedules reminders with scheduledDate less than 60 minutes (or in the past) away, defeating the cancellation design

The unscheduledReminders loop calls sgMail.send with sendAt = scheduledDate.unix() without verifying the SendGrid minimum of 60 minutes in the future (the check exists only in scheduleEmailReminder at booking time). A reminder whose scheduledDate is now+10 minutes is scheduled with a sendAt in the near past, which SendGrid processes immediately — so if a booking is cancelled right after a cron run, the cancellation (which only happens on the next 15-minute cron run) cannot win the race and the email is still sent, the exact bug being fixed. Reminders with scheduledDate < now+1h should not be scheduled via sendAt (send immediately is intended only for non-scheduled triggers).

Unused Prisma import and noisy re-indentation of commented-out code

The `Prisma` value imported from @prisma/client (line 9) is no longer used after the Prisma.BatchPayload delete logic was removed, which will fail lint/TS noUnusedLocals in stricter configs. Additionally, the diff re-indents a large block of commented-out (/* */) code in the testAction section, adding review noise and churn with no functional change; prefer leaving commented-out code untouched or deleting it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email comparisons are case-sensitive, allowing blacklist bypass and duplicates

The blacklist is lowercased (`email.toLowerCase()`) but the guest emails from input are not, and `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)` compares exactly. A guest email like `User@Example.com` bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries and can duplicate an existing attendee record (Prisma will happily create a second attendee row differing only in case), which also breaks the later `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` matching in sendAddGuestsEmails. Emails should be normalized (trim + lowercase) before all comparisons.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same blacklist bypass: blacklist entries are lowercased, but input guest emails are not, so uppercase characters evade the case-sensitive check. The additional duplicate-attendee concern does not change this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

The permission check computes `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, requiring the caller to be BOTH an admin and an owner. A user who is a team admin but not the owner is denied, even though the variable is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` and the intent is clearly OR. Team admins (who are not owners) will incorrectly receive FORBIDDEN when adding guests to team bookings. Fix to `||`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same permission-check bug: using && requires both team admin and owner status, whereas || should permit either role.

Consequently, an attendee whose email was already on the booking (i.e., not newly added) matches `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` and receives an `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a full 'you are scheduled' email with callToAction) instead of the 'guests added' notification, and blacklisted/filtered emails still influence email routing. false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses the calling user's credentials instead of the organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, ... })` use the session user, who per the permission check may be merely an attendee of the booking. The EventManager then calls `updateCalendarAttendees`, which tries to update the event on the organizer's connected calendar using the attendee's credentials. For an attendee caller this will fail or use the wrong integration, and even when the caller is the organizer but a team booking, the booking's actual host credentials (already fetched via `booking.user.credentials` include) are ignored. The event manager should be built from the booking organizer (`booking.user`), not `ctx.user`.

No guard against cancelled bookings or seat-capacity overflow

The handler adds guests without checking `booking.status` or `booking.eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot`. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (sending 'guests added' emails and calendar updates for an event that no longer exists), and for seat-based event types the attendee count can be pushed past `seatsPerTimeSlot`, corrupting the seat invariant. Validate the booking is in an active state and, for seated event types, that adding the guests does not exceed capacity.

Subject name uses attendees[0].name which may be an empty-name new guest

The organizer email subject uses `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. The addGuests handler creates attendee rows with `name: ""` for new guests, and the attendee ordering is not guaranteed, so the organizer's subject can render as 'Guests Added: 30min with  at ...' (empty name) or crash if attendees is empty. Prefer the original booker's name (the attendee who created the booking) or fall back to email.

Error path swallows the error object with a bare console.log

The catch around `sendAddGuestsEmails` only logs the literal string 'Error sending AddGuestsEmails' and discards `err`, so email delivery failures are undiagnosable in production. Log the error (ideally via the structured logger used elsewhere) so failures can be debugged.

Validation error banner never clears once shown

`isInvalidEmail` is set to true when validation fails but is only reset on Cancel. If the user corrects the emails and clicks Add again, the mutation runs while the red 'Emails must be unique and valid' banner stays visible, and if the mutation succeeds the toast plus stale error banner give contradictory feedback. Reset `isInvalidEmail` (or clear it when validation succeeds) before/inside handleAdd.

Guests array has no max length limit

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` is unbounded, so a caller can submit thousands of emails in one request. The handler then creates that many attendee rows in a single `createMany`, sends that many emails, and issues a large calendar update — an easy amplification/DoS vector for any authenticated user. Add a `.max(...)` (consistent with other booking endpoints) or enforce a limit in the handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic (read-modify-write race)

The authorize callback decrypts the backup code list, checks membership with indexOf, then nulls the used entry and writes the whole list back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the list before either writes, both pass the indexOf check, and both be accepted — a single backup code can be replayed. The update should be conditioned on the code still being present (e.g. compare-and-swap or a transaction with a where guard) so a code can only be redeemed once.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests can validate the same backup code before its consumption is persisted, allowing a one-time code to be accepted more than once.

false_positives.candidate:

The new error string is "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no UI or API to view or regenerate backup codes after setup — codes are generated once during initial 2FA setup and (after use of one) can never be replenished. A user who exhausts or loses their codes is told to do something impossible. Either a regenerate feature must be added or the message must be corrected.

Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled

The setup endpoint (which only requires the account password) writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row and returns the plaintext codes in the response, even though twoFactorEnabled is still false at this point. If the user abandons the wizard after the password step (or the QR/secret display step) and never calls enable, valid backup codes remain stored and were transmitted to the client. Any later flow that treats the presence of backupCodes as meaningful (e.g. the MissingBackupCodes vs. present-codes distinction in login) operates on codes the user may never have seen or saved. Generating codes only on successful enable (or clearing them if setup is abandoned) would be safer.

Dismissing the modal at the DisplayBackupCodes step never calls onEnable, leaving the UI switch stale

After enable succeeds the modal moves to SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes, and only the explicit Close button calls onEnable(). If the user closes the dialog via the X button, Escape, or the overlay (all handled by onOpenChange, not resetState/onEnable), two-factor is now actually enabled server-side but the parent's onEnable callback never fires, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA as disabled until reload. resetState() is also skipped, so stale backup codes/blob URL remain in component state.

The PR's core feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The e2e additions only exercise the download/copy/close buttons on the backup-code display screen; the file even carries a TODO ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the download-content/clipboard checks are TODOs. The server-side redemption logic in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts (dash stripping, single-use invalidation, MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode paths) is untested, so a regression in the only code path that verifies backup codes would go unnoticed.

Backup code is consumed even if login subsequently fails

The used backup code is nulled and persisted in the database immediately after the indexOf match, before the rest of the authorize function runs (team checks, password-policy role validation, JWT/session creation). If anything after that point throws or the sign-in callback redirects (e.g. an INACTIVE_ADMIN downgrade or an error during token issuance), the user has permanently lost a backup code without gaining access. The invalidation should be tied to successful sign-in, not to passing the code check.

The login form in apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx is rendered with noValidate, so the native minLength={10}/maxLength={11}/required attributes on the BackupCode TextField never trigger. The zod schema also does not include backupCode (the object is .passthrough()), so a user can submit an empty or malformed backup code; the empty string is falsy on the server, so the request silently falls into the TOTP branch and returns a confusing "second factor required" error instead of a validation message telling the user to enter the code.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

This is a public API contract change shipped as a 'bug fix' with no changelog/migration note or versioning; consumers should be notified or the field kept backwards compatible.

Any later flow that reconstructs the CalendarEvent from the DB (cancel, reschedule, bookingReminder, confirm handler) sets `destinationCalendar: [booking.destinationCalendar]`, dropping the other hosts' calendars. The multi-host support therefore only works on the initial create; the deletion/update paths rely solely on references, and any path that re-derives behavior from `evt.destinationCalendar` (e.g. the Meet fallback in EventManager) will behave differently after a reload.

`teamDestinationCalendars` is populated inside the `users.slice(1).map(...)` callback with `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)`. If the same user's calendar is also the eventType/organizer destinationCalendar it gets duplicated in `evt.destinationCalendar`, causing `createAllCalendarEvents` to attempt creating the event twice on the same calendar (two Google events / duplicate references). No de-duplication by credentialId/externalId is performed before `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`.

In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"` but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (to add the hangout link to the description) uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the `|| "primary"` fallback. When the event was created on the primary calendar because no destination matched the credentialId, the patch targets `calendarId: undefined` and fails silently, so the Meet link is never added to the event description.

No tests for the multi-destination-calendar behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This is a large behavioral change (destinationCalendar becomes an array, create/update/delete fan out over multiple calendar references and credentials, new DB fallback for credentials) touching ~20 files including payment webhooks and cancellation. At minimum, unit tests for `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` with multiple destination calendars and mixed credential availability, plus a regression test for the Google Meet empty-destinationCalendar case, are needed before merging.

This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
