`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` never awaits the returned promises. With the now-async `getCalendar`, each callback suspends at the first await and the surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch any errors thrown inside (rejections become unhandled promise rejections, not logged). The function then proceeds to send the reschedule email and return success while external calendar/video deletions may still be in flight (or fail silently), so users' external calendars can keep the old event even though the booking was already set to CANCELLED in the DB at line 67. The same pattern exists in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts line 125 and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx line 553 (requestReschedule). Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: async callbacks passed to forEach produce unawaited promises, allowing cleanup to run in the background and bypass surrounding try/catch error handling. It also recommends the same Promise.all with map fix. Its narrower focus on event deletions does not change the semantic match.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic import() calls are invoked eagerly, defeating the stated purpose of the PR

The appStore object is a module-level object literal whose property values are `import("./applecalendar")` etc. These import() calls all execute as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is first imported — every app module begins loading immediately, in parallel. The PR description says it makes app imports async/lazy, but no app loading is actually deferred; only the *await* is deferred. To make loading truly lazy, the store should hold factory functions (`() => import("./applecalendar")`) that are called on demand, otherwise this change adds promise indirection with no startup-time benefit (and a burst of simultaneous module loads on first import).

getCalendarCredentials now stores a Promise in the `calendar` field, silently changing its contract

`getCalendarCredentials` calls `getCalendar(credential)` without awaiting, so each returned item's `calendar` property is now a `Promise<Calendar | null>` rather than a `Calendar | null`. The internal consumer `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`, but `getCalendarCredentials` is an exported function; any other caller that uses `item.calendar` directly (e.g. calling `calendar.listCalendars()` or checking `if (!calendar)`) now operates on a Promise, which is always truthy, so null-checks stop working and method calls will fail at runtime with no TypeScript error if the consumer widened the type. The promise should be either awaited in `getCalendarCredentials` (making it async) or explicitly typed so callers know to await it.

Static app imports in EventManager and other core files undermine the async appStore refactor

While appStore was converted to dynamic imports, `packages/core/EventManager.ts` still statically imports `FAKE_DAILY_CREDENTIAL` from `@calcom/app-store/dailyvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter`, `handleCancelBooking.ts` statically imports from dailyvideo and zapier app packages, and `videoClient.ts` statically imports `getDailyAppKeys` from `@calcom/app-store/dailyvideo/lib/getDailyAppKeys`. These static imports pull the dailyvideo and zapier app modules (and their dependency trees) into every bundle/serverless function that includes core, negating the code-splitting the PR intends. At minimum this inconsistency should be noted or resolved, otherwise the refactor provides no bundle-size benefit for the booking flow.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

test_basic relies on a fixed 0.1s sleep for the flusher thread to observe the drift change

There is no synchronization guaranteeing the thread reached the read of `current_drift` or completed the flush/produce within 100ms, so the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking can flake on slow/loaded CI. false_positives.candidate:
Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and resources

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, an unhealthy process is `process.kill()`-ed and a replacement is immediately started via `_create_process_for_shards`, but the old process object is never `join()`-ed. In production (spawn mode) each killed process becomes a zombie until the parent exits, and its `SpansBuffer` (with its Redis connection pool) is dropped from `self.buffers[process_index]` without being closed, leaking connections. Since restarts can happen repeatedly (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index), a consumer running for a long time can accumulate zombies and leaked Redis connections. The old process should be joined/cleaned up before or after starting the replacement.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is defined but never called anywhere; the restart path uses `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. Dead code invites confusion about which restart entrypoint to use and should be removed.

Per-process restart counters never reset, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer

`self.process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented and never reset, even after a process has been running healthily for a long time. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, a process that legitimately crashed 11 times over months of uptime (e.g. transient Redis outages) will cause `_ensure_processes_alive` to raise RuntimeError and take down the whole consumer. The counter should be reset once the replacement process has been observed healthy for some period. This was a pre-existing flaw for the single process, but multiplying the number of processes multiplies the probability of hitting it.

Tests only cover the threading (produce_to_pipe) path, never the multiprocessing path

Both consumer tests and test_flusher.py inject `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` and `partial` instead of the spawn-based `multiprocessing.Process` with `run_with_initialized_sentry`. None of the new multi-process behavior (process-per-shard spawn, argument pickling of per-shard SpansBuffer and shared Values, process restart in `_ensure_processes_alive`, join/terminate of real processes) is exercised. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts on dicts/counts, not that processes actually work. A regression in the spawn path (e.g. a pickling error in the new per-shard buffer or the new `shards` argument) would not be caught.

max_processes default of None means one process per shard, contradicting documented default of 1

`SpanFlusher.__init__` treats `max_processes=None` as `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, i.e. one process per shard. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option documents "Defaults to 1", and its click default is 1, so CLI-driven deployments get 1; but any other instantiation path that omits the argument (as all existing direct callers in tests and code do) silently spawns one process per assigned partition, each of which re-imports sentry/Django under spawn. This is a significant behavioral/memory difference depending on call path, and the docstring does not mention it. The default should be consistent (e.g. 1) or the behavior documented.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as abstract method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations

The new `int order()` method on the public `CryptoProvider` interface has no default implementation. Any existing external implementation of `CryptoProvider` (e.g. custom providers used by downstream projects or the adapter SPI consumers) will fail to load at runtime once keycloak-common is upgraded: ServiceLoader instantiation throws ServiceConfigurationError with AbstractMethodError on first call to order(), or the class no longer compiles. Since CryptoProvider already uses `default` methods elsewhere in this same interface (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes), `order()` should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) to preserve binary and source compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The new order() method on CryptoProvider is abstract, which breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations. The candidate also suggests making it a default method.

false_positives.candidate:
integerToBytes silently truncates out-of-range signature integers

In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes keeps only the low `qLength` bytes when the decoded BigInteger is longer than the expected half-signature length (`qLength < bytes.length` branch takes the *last* bytes of toByteArray(), which for a positive value drops the most significant bytes). A DER signature whose r or s exceeds the curve order would be silently accepted and mangled rather than rejected, producing a signature that could verify against a different value than what was signed in length-mismatch scenarios. Validation (throwing when the value does not fit in qLength) would be the safe behavior for signature conversion.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset queryset slicing raises an exception, so the 'advanced pagination' path always fails

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices: it raises `AssertionError` ("Negative indexing is not supported") unless a negative step is used, and with a step it's not valid SQL OFFSET semantics. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any client that sends a cursor with a negative offset while using optimized_pagination=true will get a 500 error; the feature can never return data.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator slices a Django queryset with a negative offset, and Django raises an AssertionError because it does not support negative indexing.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets to 0 instead of rejecting them

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior for all existing paginators (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc.). Previously, a malformed/corrupted cursor with a negative offset on a forward page would surface as an error from queryset slicing; now it is silently clamped to 0 and the client receives the first page of results while believing it is on a later page. This masks cursor corruption and can produce silently wrong data (e.g., duplicate rows already seen). For is_prev cursors the negative offset is still passed through, so it will raise an exception from the ORM — inconsistent behavior between the two directions. The correct fix is to validate and reject negative offsets (as OffsetPaginator and ChainPaginator do with BadPaginationError).

New undocumented 'optimized_pagination' query parameter and superuser-gated paginator add no functionality and can 500

The endpoint adds an undocumented, EXPERIMENTAL-status query parameter `optimized_pagination` that switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True for superusers/global-access users. Since the advanced path only activates for negative cursor offsets and that path always raises an exception when slicing the queryset, this flag is a purely additive way for privileged clients to trigger server errors. There is no test coverage for the new parameter or the new paginator, and no documentation of the parameter's contract. Additionally, the gating on is_superuser/has_global_access suggests a security boundary, but the comment in the paginator ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') reveals the queryset is already org-scoped — the permission gate provides no actual protection and is misleading.

is_prev length check uses raw (possibly negative) offset, so the trailing-row trim never fires for advanced cursors

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when a previous-page cursor with a value is used together with a negative offset (the advanced path), the check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares against the original (negative) offset, while the results were fetched using `start_offset = cursor.offset` and `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`. The length of the fetched slice can never equal a negative-plus-limit sum in the intended way, so the extra boundary row is never trimmed, resulting in off-by-one duplicate/missing rows at page boundaries for previous-page navigation.

Comment in Cursor implies negative offsets are a supported general feature

The added comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets are allowed for 'advanced pagination scenarios', but nothing in Cursor.from_string or anywhere else validates or supports them coherently: other paginators (SequencePaginator, OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator) explicitly assert or raise on negative offsets, while BasePaginator-based ones now either clamp them silently or crash depending on is_prev. The comment documents behavior that does not exist and will mislead maintainers.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the whole-function lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, which (coarsely) serialized index creation. With the lock now only taken around the final map write, two concurrent callers (e.g. two gRPC Search requests hitting getOrCreateIndex for the same NamespacedResource, or a watch event arriving during a first search) can both observe GetIndex()==nil and both run BuildIndex for the same key. For file-based indexes both will call bleve.New with the same directory (filepath.Join(Root, namespace, resource.group)); the second call fails or clobbers the first, and the cache ends up with one index while the other caller holds a stale index object that will never receive watch updates. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go already has a TODO acknowledging the per-key blocking need; the lock removal makes this a live bug rather than a theoretical one. A per-key singleflight/mutex is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same race in BuildIndex: the lock now covers only the final cache assignment instead of the whole function, so concurrent callers can build duplicate indexes for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

TotalDocs reads b.cache without the cache lock while BuildIndex writes it

Previously the coarse lock at least serialized map writes across all builds; now an unsynchronized map read concurrent with a map write can panic the process with 'concurrent map read and map write' or return inconsistent totals. Take b.cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while BuildIndex writes to the map concurrently, which risks a concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate attributes the concurrent writes to errgroup workers rather than the event watcher goroutine, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown require Python 3.13

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, but Queue.shutdown() and the ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs (3.11/3.12) this raises AttributeError at shutdown time (silently swallowed by the try/except, so workers are never told to stop and blocked worker threads never exit), and the `except queue.ShutDown` handlers would fail to even import-resolve at runtime. The graceful shutdown path is broken on supported Python versions; use a sentinel/Event-based approach instead.

Failed messages are marked completed and their offsets committed, silently dropping them

OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a `finally` block, so when result_processor raises, the offset is still considered complete and the commit loop will commit past it. Combined with the fact that ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows all exceptions (logs only), any message that fails processing (e.g. DB error, bad subscription data) is permanently lost with no retry and no DLQ — the offset is committed so it will never be redelivered. The existing test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts this drop-on-failure behavior. There should be a retry/DLQ path or the offset should remain outstanding (blocking commit) on failure so the message is redelivered.

Queues are unbounded — no backpressure despite docstring claim, risk of unbounded memory growth

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after enqueueing, so the arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as it can. If processing (DB-backed result handling) is slower than consumption, queues grow without limit, holding decoded messages and their Message objects in memory until OOM. The class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' guarantee is false as implemented. Either set maxsize and block/propagate backpressure in submit(), or bound total in-flight items.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain, losing final offset commits

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(), which is what drains the worker queues. Any messages processed after the last commit-loop iteration (up to the entire remaining queue contents at shutdown) will be processed but never committed. On restart/rebalance those messages are redelivered and reprocessed, which for non-idempotent result handling means duplicate side effects. The correct order is: stop accepting new work, drain queues, do a final get_committable_offsets/commit, then stop the commit thread.

join() unconditionally calls close(), causing double shutdown and ignoring its timeout

Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close() then join() on strategies. Here join() calls close() again: shutdown_event.set() and commit_thread.join() are harmless, but queue_pool.shutdown() runs a second time — each Queue.shutdown() (on 3.13) raises ValueError on already-shutdown queues (swallowed by the broad except, hiding errors), and worker.join() is called again. Additionally the `timeout` parameter of join() is accepted but never used, so a stuck worker blocks shutdown for the full 5s join regardless. join() should simply wait (using its timeout) for work to drain, not re-run shutdown.

Worker thread death permanently stalls offset commits for its queue

If an OrderedQueueWorker thread exits for any reason other than a clean shutdown — e.g. an exception raised by metrics.gauge or the sentry_sdk transaction wrapper inside the finally block, or a non-Exception BaseException from result_processor — the thread dies, but all offsets of items still sitting in its queue remain in OffsetTracker.outstanding forever. get_committable_offsets will never advance past the smallest such offset, so commits for that partition stop entirely, backpressure-free consumption continues enqueueing into a queue nobody reads, and memory grows until the process is killed. There is no liveness check or worker restart.

Arroyo Commit callable invoked from a background thread concurrently with the consumer thread

The commit loop thread calls the arroyo Commit function (which ends up calling consumer commit / interacting with consumer state) once per second, while the StreamProcessor's main thread concurrently polls the consumer and may itself commit or rebalance. Arroyo strategies normally call commit from the processing (main) thread; calling it from an unsynchronized background thread risks racing with the consumer during rebalances/shutdown and can produce errors or commits of stale offsets. This needs verification against arroyo's thread-safety contract, or the commit should be marshalled back to the strategy thread (e.g. via poll()).

The test asserts that 20 arbitrary group keys hashed with Python's builtin hash() (which is salted per process for str) land on exactly all 3 queues. With random salt it is possible (though unlikely) that fewer than 3 distinct indices are hit, making the test flaky across runs. Asserting `>= 2` or using fixed deterministic keys would be robust.

A sentry_sdk transaction is started for every single message in every worker

OrderedQueueWorker wraps each individual result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction. At production uptime-result volumes this creates and discards a transaction object per message (20 queues × full throughput), adding significant per-message overhead and, if any transaction sampling is enabled, flooding Sentry with events. The batched-parallel mode wraps batches, not items; this should be a span or sampled/omitted entirely.

The comment claims 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. Any request that reaches this branch (cursor with negative offset, `optimized_pagination=true`, privileged user) will produce a 500 instead of a page of results. Since cursors are client-supplied strings parsed by `Cursor.from_string`, a negative offset is trivially craftable, making this a denial-of-service on the endpoint.

Combined with `Cursor.from_string` accepting any integer offset from the client, a malicious cursor such as `0:-5:1` on any endpoint using BasePaginator subclasses will hit Django's negative-slicing AssertionError (or, for list-backed paginators, silently return wrong rows). true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

The audit log endpoint sorts by `-datetime` and previously used `DateTimePaginator`, which converts datetimes to epoch-millis ints for cursor keys. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` is copied from the plain `Paginator` and does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` on the raw attribute; when the attribute is a `datetime`, `math.floor`/`int()` raise `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware...`/`type error`. So the optimized path crashes whenever it needs to compute an item key (any request with results). Additionally, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, whereas `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` converts the millis value back into a timezone-aware datetime for the SQL comparison — the optimized path would compare a float against a datetime column and break the query. The paginator is simply not usable for this endpoint's data type.

The new eviction block pops `span_count - 1000` members off the set whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, permanently dropping those span payloads before they are ever flushed to the `buffered-spans` topic. The Python-side `max_segment_spans` guard (which skipped the segment and logged an error) was removed from `_load_segment_data` without replacement. The 1000 limit is hardcoded in Lua, is inconsistent with the Python `max_segment_spans = 1001` default, and there is no metric increment, log, or counter when eviction occurs — segments above 1000 spans will be silently truncated, making the data loss invisible in monitoring. Eviction also uses `zpopmin` (lowest end timestamp), meaning the oldest spans of a segment vanish, potentially including the root/segment span that later code (`is_segment` detection, redirect handling) depends on.

The script now calls `zcard`/`zunionstore` where it previously called `scard`/`sunionstore`. During a rolling deploy, old-version processes still write span payloads via `sadd`/`sunionstore` while new-version processes read them with `zcard`, so existing set-typed keys are invisible to the new logic (`zcard` on a set key returns a WRONGTYPE error in Redis, actually failing the EVALSHA call entirely). There is no migration or versioning strategy, so deploying this will produce errors/data loss for any in-flight traces buffered before the deploy. `buffer.py` also changed `sadd`→`zadd` and `sscan`→`zscan` symmetrically, but mixed-version operation during rollout is not handled.

The redirect-following loop bound was cut from 10000 to 1000 with no explanation in the PR description and no constant shared with Python. The original comment noted the limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not join correctly; reducing to 1000 tightens that failure mode. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with `set_span_id` pointing at an intermediate node and the span is written to the wrong buffer key, splitting a segment — silently, since the returned `redirect_depth` metric is the only signal. If this reduction was intentional (e.g. to bound Redis script runtime), it should be documented and covered by a test; neither exists.

A new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter changes which paginator implementation and behavior (including negative-offset support) the audit log endpoint uses, but it is not documented in the API schema, not covered by any endpoint test, and the behavior difference is invisible to clients. The permission gate uses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` (owner/manager) or superuser, but audit logs are sensitive security data and the 'advanced' path offers no clear benefit while introducing the crash bugs above. This change is also entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (span buffer optimization), making it easy to miss in review.

The call passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to `self.paginate(...)`. Whether this kwarg reaches `OptimizedCursorPaginator.__init__` depends on the endpoint base class's `paginate` implementation forwarding arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`; the standard `paginate` in sentry's API base constructs the paginator with a fixed set of arguments (queryset, order_by, etc.). If it does not forward the kwarg, this raises a TypeError (500) on every optimized request; if it does forward it, the default `enable_advanced_features=False` still enables the negative-offset branch only for this flag combination, which no test exercises. Either way there is no test covering this endpoint's new code path.

The core behavioral changes of this PR — segments exceeding 1000 spans being truncated via `zpopmin`, the removal of the `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data`, and the set→sorted-set conversion — have no test coverage. All existing tests use tiny traces (4-5 spans) with identical timestamps, so they cannot catch wrong sort scores, eviction of the wrong members, or eviction of the root span. A test that builds a segment of >1000 spans with distinct `end_timestamp_precise` values and asserts which spans survive is needed before this data-lossy change can be merged.

In `build_queryset`, the branch that converts an existing `-{key}` ordering back to ascending assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. While pre-existing, the new negative-offset/OptimizedCursorPaginator work sits directly on top of this path and the diff touches the surrounding function, so the bug now affects the new paginator too: a prev-cursor request on a queryset already ordered by `-datetime` will not have its ordering flipped to ASC, producing incorrectly ordered (and thus incorrectly paginated) results. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by plain underscore concatenation: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Both userUID and name/parent are attacker-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores, so two distinct (user, action, name, parent) tuples can produce the same key (e.g. uid "a", action "x", name "b_c" vs uid "a", action "x", name "b", parent "c" with an underscore shift). Worse, the key shares the "<ns>.perm_" prefix space with userPermCacheKey(ns, userUID, action), so a denial entry for one user/action tuple can be read as another user's permission set (or vice versa) if components line up — in Check, permCache.Get is keyed by the same scheme and the denial cache shares the same underlying cache.Cache instance. The candidate's extra point about collisions with the permission cache prefix is additional detail and does not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache reintroduces the exact bug this PR is meant to fix

The new negative cache caches a deny decision for shortCacheTTL (30s) keyed on (namespace, user, action, resource name, parent folder), and there is no invalidation when permissions or resources change. Scenario: a user requests a dashboard that does not yet exist / they have no permission for (Check returns deny and the entry is written at line 154). The user then creates that dashboard or folder (or an admin grants access). The very next Check for the same resource hits the denial entry at line 117 and is denied for up to 30 seconds, with no DB fallback. This is precisely the 'creator can't access the dashboard they just created' failure the PR description says it fixes — it is now bounded to ~30s instead of removed. Same for newly granted permissions: access is delayed by up to 30s. Consider invalidating the denial entry on writes, keying it more coarsely with shorter TTL, or not caching denials when the resource was simply absent from the scope map.

No test that a deny decision actually writes the denial cache entry

TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' case only verifies that a manually pre-populated permDenialCache entry causes a deny. There is no test asserting that after Check returns Allowed=false from a DB query, the service writes the denial entry (service.go:154) and that a subsequent Check for the same resource short-circuits without hitting the store. This is the core new behavior of the PR (negative caching) and its write path is untested; a regression that never writes the entry (making the whole feature a no-op) would pass the current suite.

When the denial cache is hit, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit) even though the permission cache was not consulted. Additionally, when cached permissions exist but evaluate to deny, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" (line 137) despite the perm cache actually being hit. Both skew the cache-hit-rate metric in opposite directions, making it unusable for evaluating whether the caching changes are effective.

Deny path with cached permissions always re-queries the DB, defeating singleflight in common case

When a user has cached permissions that don't cover the requested resource (a very common deny case for legitimate users, e.g. dashboard they don't own), Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and performs a full DB permission query, and a denial entry is only written afterward. For users with genuinely no permission for the action at all, getIdentityPermissions returns an empty/stale-cached scope map which is re-fetched and re-set into permCache each time before checkPermission denies. The permCache is refreshed with identical data on every request for such users (singleflight only dedups concurrent, not sequential calls). Consider not re-setting permCache when the fetched map is identical, or caching 'no permissions for action' explicitly, to avoid write amplification on the hot deny path.

Previously the delete affected-rows and selection were one statement so this could not happen. A safer termination condition is len(ids) == 0, not affected == 0.

Since object names are unbounded user-controlled values, this creates unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus (one metric series per deleted object name) and inconsistent labeling versus the failure path on line 103. It should pass `options.Kind`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: the Delete metrics recording passes name where the other methods pass options.Kind. The candidate's cardinality point is extra detail on that same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes

In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to the legacy store derives its 10-second-timeout context from the incoming request context (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The parent `ctx` is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request that triggered the write completes, so the legacy write is very likely aborted immediately rather than running for the intended 10 seconds. This defeats the purpose of the 'safe measure' write to legacy: legacy storage will silently miss writes whenever the client disconnects or the request handler returns quickly, leaving the two stores permanently divergent with no error surfaced. The goroutine should use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context) as the parent.

Storage failures recorded under the legacy metric in Create and Update

In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129), the error path when the unified Storage call fails calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. This records a failed, zero-length 'legacy' operation that never happened, corrupting legacy-store error-rate and duration metrics. It should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` to match the Delete and DeleteCollection error paths.

Tests spawn unmocked async legacy calls that can panic or race in goroutines

Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a background goroutine, but the tests never wait for it and in several success cases never stub it: TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection set up no `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection` mock expectations, and TestMode3_Create's second case stubs only the legacy mock. testify's `mock.Mock` panics on calls to methods with no expected call, so these goroutines can panic non-deterministically after the subtest finishes, causing flaky suite crashes. Additionally, since the goroutine's error is never returned or awaited, no test actually verifies that the legacy write happens, times out, or that legacy failures are correctly logged/metriced — the core behavior of this PR is untested.

No retry, queue, or error surfacing for failed legacy writes

All legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines: if `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete` fails (or the derived context is cancelled per the context issue), the error is only swallowed into a metric — there is no logging of the failure, no retry, and no reconciliation mechanism. Once mode 3 is the default, any transient legacy failure leaves the legacy database permanently out of sync, which matters because legacy Grafana APIs and other code paths still read from legacy storage. At minimum the goroutines should log the legacy error, and the team should confirm a backfill/reconciliation job exists before enabling mode 3.

If that second pass is not a no-op on an already-interpolated expression (e.g. a variable value that itself contains `$`, escaped characters, or format-dependent multi-value expansion), the executed query would be double-interpolated and incorrect. All new tests ('Interpolates queries before execution' in both querySplitting.test.ts and shardQuerySplitting.test.ts) replace runQuery with a jest mock, so they only assert that the pre-interpolation happened and cannot detect that the real runQuery interpolates again. $__range guard in querySupportsSplitting now runs against the interpolated expression

querySupportsSplitting explicitly refuses to split queries containing a range variable because $__range must be interpolated on the backend against the split time range. The guard isQueryWithRangeVariable now inspects the interpolated expr: in any context where the frontend template service resolves $__range (for example when scopedVars carries a range variable, or via a dashboard variable whose value is '$__range'), the literal '$__range' no longer appears in the expr, the query is misclassified as splittable, and it gets executed with a per-chunk $__range baked in from the wrong (already-replaced) range, producing wrong data. Previously the check ran on the raw expression. The guard should be evaluated on the pre-interpolation expression, or interpolation must demonstrably preserve $__range.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

Device limit check is not atomic (count-then-insert race)

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs a COUNT query and then a separate INSERT/UPSERT, without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from multiple new devices can all observe a count below the limit and all insert, overshooting `device_limit` arbitrarily under load. The check and insert (or the update fallback) need to be done atomically (e.g. in a transaction with a row lock, or by enforcing the limit inside the upsert statement) for the limit to actually hold.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition. The device count check and the insert are not atomic, so concurrent requests can exceed the device limit. Both suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache marker set before the store call masks the device-limit error for 29 minutes

In `tagDeviceUI`, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If the store call then fails — including with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` or any transient DB error — the cache still holds the device key for up to 29 minutes, so all subsequent requests for that device return nil early from the cache. This means the limit error is reported only on the first request per device per cache window (inconsistent enforcement), and transient DB failures are silently swallowed after the first attempt. The cache entry should be set only after a successful store write, or rolled back on error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: in tagDeviceUI the cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so when ErrDeviceLimitReached occurs the cache entry stays and later requests bypass the limit for 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous auth now performs a blocking DB write on the request path

The previous code tagged anonymous devices in a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, decoupling it from request latency. This change makes `Authenticate` call `TagDevice` synchronously on the request context, so every anonymous request from a device not in the 29-minute local cache adds a database roundtrip (and a COUNT query plus INSERT/UPDATE when a device limit is configured) to login/authn latency. Under load on anonymous-enabled instances this measurably slows requests and adds DB pressure; the original async design existed for this reason and no replacement (e.g. async with error propagation for the limit case only) was provided.

ErrDeviceLimitReached returned raw to authn produces an opaque auth failure

When the device limit is reached, `Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` directly as the authentication error. There is no mapping to an HTTP status or user-facing message, so a user exceeding the device limit will get a generic internal auth error (likely 500) with only "device limit reached" in logs, instead of a clear 4xx with an explanatory message. The error should be wrapped/mapped to a proper authn error type before being returned.

anonymousDeviceLimit always serialized, contradicting the optional TS type

The Go DTO field `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`, so the frontend settings JSON always contains `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0` when unlimited, while the TypeScript type declares it as `number | undefined`. Code distinguishing "no limit" via `undefined` (e.g. `if (config.anonymousDeviceLimit)`) works, but code using `=== undefined` or relying on the key's absence will misbehave. The Go field should be a pointer with `omitempty` (like `TokenExpirationDayLimit`-style optional fields) to match the declared contract.

New device_limit setting is undocumented and the PR description is a template

A new `device_limit` key is added under `[auth.anonymous]`, but the configuration documentation (configure-security/configure-authentication docs in grafana/grafana) is not updated in this PR, and the PR description still contains unfilled template placeholders ("[Add a description...]", "Fixes #"). Users cannot discover or correctly use the setting, and the intended semantics (0 = unlimited, expiry window of 30 days) are only visible in code.

The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback list can contain the literal symbol of an invalid locale and mixes string/symbol locales

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` assumes SiteSetting.default_locale is always a symbolizable valid locale; if it is ever nil or an unsupported value, `nil.to_sym` raises NoMethodError inside every I18n lookup via the fallback chain, breaking all translations for the request. Additionally, `locale` may be a string or symbol depending on caller (I18n.locale vs raw keys), and `uniq` on mixed types ("de" vs :de) will not deduplicate, potentially causing the same locale to be tried twice per lookup. Normalize all entries with to_sym before uniq and guard against nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments are about String vs Symbol locales not being normalized, which leads to duplicate handling. The golden comment is about double-loading in the check/load logic. The candidate makes the same point about the fallback list, where uniq fails to dedupe mixed types, and recommends normalizing with to_sym. The location differs, but the golden says the concern also applies elsewhere in the PR, so the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Translation cache key ignores fallback locales, causing stale/wrong cached translations

I18n.translate caches results under a key of "#{key}#{config.locale}#{backend.object_id}". With fallbacks enabled, the result of a translation now also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (e.g. translating key X in locale :es may return the :es string, or fall back to the site default locale's or English string). Because the cache key only contains the requested locale, a cached fallback result will be reused even after the site's default_locale changes (or, on a multi-process deployment where the cache lives per process, results computed under an old default_locale persist until the cache is evicted or the process restarts). Users would see translations from the wrong locale until restart. The cache key should include the fallback chain (e.g. I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].join) or the cache must be cleared when default_locale changes.

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but overrides [], making it a broken/unused Hash

FallbackLocaleList inherits from Hash but its `[]` ignores all hash state and always computes [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]. Any other Hash behavior (each, key?, merge, dup, defaults handling in i18n's Fallbacks code) will not see any entries and will behave as an empty hash. i18n-gem code that manipulates the fallbacks object as a hash (e.g. I18n.fallbacks.merge!, inspecting it, or copying it) will silently do nothing or produce wrong results. Either use a plain object that duck-types `[]`/`ensure_loaded!` without the Hash superclass, or actually store the computed fallback chain in the hash so Hash semantics stay consistent.

ensure_loaded! only runs for web requests; fallback locales are never loaded in jobs/mailers

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is called only in ApplicationController#set_locale. Background jobs, mailers, and any other entry point that sets I18n.locale (e.g. Discourse's job locale handling, I18n.locale = user locale) will use the fallback chain without the fallback locales being loaded into the backend. Because translate_accelerator forces explicit loading (load_translations ignores empty args) and only loads config.locale inside translate, lookups for the fallback locales (site default locale, or :en) will miss and silently return the next fallback — meaning users get English strings instead of the site-default-locale translations in emails and scheduled jobs. The ensure_loaded! should be invoked wherever I18n.locale is set outside controllers, or translate should load all fallback locales.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

record_for_host compares a possibly mixed-case referer host against lowercased stored hosts

With `sidekiq_options retry: false` the exception is swallowed and, more importantly, it aborts processing of the remaining feed items in the same run, so topics after the offending item are never imported until the next hour. true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. false_positives.candidate:
RSS feed content is stored and rendered as raw HTML without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method: raw_html, which makes Post#cook return raw unchanged (app/models/post.rb line 133). When called from the PollFeed path (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35-36), `contents` is the raw feed item content with only CGI.unescapeHTML applied — no HTML sanitization occurs. The embed view (app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19) then renders these posts with `raw post.cooked`. Any <script>, inline event handlers, or other malicious markup in the external feed is stored verbatim and executed in the Discourse origin for every visitor of the embedded page, allowing a compromised or malicious feed to hijack Discourse sessions/perform CSRF. The import_remote path limits tags/attributes via readability, but the feed path has no such filtering; contents should be sanitized (e.g. via Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

feed_key is dead code; no conditional-fetch deduplication is implemented

The `feed_key` method (used nowhere) and its 'feed-modified:' redis key suggest the intent was to skip polling when the feed has not changed (e.g. via Last-Modified/ETag), but poll_feed unconditionally re-opens the feed URL and re-processes every item every hour. Either remove the dead method or wire it up to store/compare the feed's modified time so polling is skipped when unchanged.

setnx followed by separate expire is not atomic

retrieved_recently? uses $redis.setnx and then a separate $redis.expire. If the process dies (or redis restarts) between the two calls, the key 'retrieved:<url>' exists with no TTL and permanently blocks retrieval for that embed URL until manual redis intervention. Use a single SET key value EX 60 NX (or setex-style) operation so the TTL is set atomically with the key creation.

On re-import of an existing embed, `post = embed.post` is used without a nil check before `PostRevisor.new(post)` and `embed.update_column`. If the topic's post was deleted (or post_id points to a removed record — the association has no dependent handling and nothing destroys the TopicEmbed when its post is destroyed), the poll job will raise NoMethodError on nil every run for that URL. Guard for a missing post (and consider destroying the TopicEmbed alongside the post).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

The class now defines `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and then redefines `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. Ruby silently discards the first definition (with a 'method redefined' warning in some modes), and both have the same arity so callers passing width and height as separate integers will now hit the second definition and produce a broken dimension string like "640x480" vs "1024-768"-style concatenation issues... concretely, a caller invoking downsize(from, to, 100, 75) now gets dimensions "100" passed to ImageMagick (75 is bound to opts), producing wrong output rather than an error. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. downsize is defined twice, the second definition overrides the first width/height version, and callers that pass separate width and height arguments break.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client-side limit ignores SiteSetting max image/attachment sizes

The client-side upload validation previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'] (i.e. max_image_size_kb / max_attachment_size_kb) but now hardcodes 10MB. This breaks validation in both directions: on sites where the admin set a lower limit (e.g. 4MB), oversized files pass the client check and only fail on the server with a confusing generic error; and the hardcoded 10MB cap cannot be raised by admins. The same hardcode in the 413 handler (line 246) shows users a wrong maximum size in the error message. The stated goal of the PR (allow large images that the server will downsize) is undermined because the client still blocks any image over 10MB and, worse, blocks images over the (possibly small) configured limit that the new server-side downsizing was meant to accept — the client check should be relaxed or removed for images, not fixed at 10MB.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same problem as the golden comment. It names the hardcoded 10MB limit, notes that it ignores the max_<type>_size_kb site settings, and points out that the 413 handler has the same hardcode.

false_positives.candidate:
In-place downsize: convert is run with input and output as the same file path

OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...) executes ImageMagick's `convert /tmp/xxx /tmp/xxx`, i.e. the source and destination are the same path. ImageMagick reads the input lazily and can truncate/corrupt the file while writing, or fail outright, depending on format and buffering. The result can be a corrupted or zero-byte upload. The downsized output should be written to a separate temp file and then replace the original.

Animated GIFs lose animation and animated path is never selected for uploads

The animated-image branch in OptimizedImage.optimize is chosen only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but `tempfile.path` for an uploaded file is a Tempfile path with no .gif extension (e.g. /tmp/d discourse-upload...). So animated GIFs always go through `convert #{from}[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame, silently destroying animation. Additionally, `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is passed, but the actual check inside optimize tests the file path's extension, not the flag, so the setting has no effect here. Files with no recognizable animation possible (corrupt images) will also make `convert` fail repeatedly (see next finding).

Downsize loop ignores failures and still submits the oversized file

The while loop decrements `attempt` but never checks the return value of OptimizedImage.downsize, which returns false when convert fails (corrupt image, missing ImageMagick, etc.). On failure the file size never changes, so the loop pointlessly shells out 5 times and then passes the still-oversized file to Upload.create_for, which will reject it with a generic error. The loop should break out and fail fast (or surface a clear error) when downsize returns false.

API URL download cap hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

FileHelper.download for API-provided URLs now uses a fixed 10.megabytes cap instead of SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes. On sites where max_image_size_kb (or max_attachment_size_kb) is configured above 10MB, valid API uploads are now truncated/fail at 10MB with no way to configure it; below 10MB, non-image downloads are no longer bounded by the image setting at all. The cap should be derived from the relevant setting (e.g. [max_image_size_kb, max_attachment_size_kb].max) rather than hardcoded.

Downsized image keeps original filename but stored sha/filesize mismatch metadata assumptions

After downsizing, the upload is created with the original `filename` and the new (smaller) tempfile.size, but the content no longer matches the file the user chose; more importantly, uploads of type where FileHelper.is_image? matches by extension (e.g. .svg) will run ImageMagick `convert` on an SVG with "80%" geometry, which either rasterizes the SVG (destroying its vector nature) or fails. SVGs should be excluded from the downsize path the same way OptimizedImage.create_for special-cases .svg.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash

Two concrete problems: (1) `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` returns nil when the logged-in user has no topic_users row for that topic (e.g. they received the email via a mention/watch category without ever visiting, or the row was cleaned up); `tu.notification_level` on the next line then raises NoMethodError, producing a 500 instead of a graceful response. It should use TopicUser.change or handle the nil case. (2) Because the toggle is a side effect of a GET, simply refreshing or re-visiting the emailed link flips the user back and forth between muted and regular, and any third-party page can trigger the state change for a logged-in user via an /link (CSRF via GET). The mutation should be a POST/PUT (or done through the Ember route with an explicit action), not performed on every GET.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says that TopicUser.find_by returns nil when no record exists and that the call on tu.notification_level then raises NoMethodError. This is the same nil pointer issue the golden comment describes.

false_positives.candidate:

The unsubscribe action sets notification_level directly on the TopicUser AR object and calls save!, instead of using TopicUser.change. TopicUser.change is the canonical path that also stamps notifications_changed_at, notifications_reason_id, publishes the MessageBus notification_level_change event to the user's open tabs, and handles record creation races. The rewritten `unsubscribe_link` locale string now interpolates both %{user_preferences_url} and %{unsubscribe_url}. Email::MessageBuilder#body and #html_part call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args) whenever @opts[:add_unsubscribe_link] is true, but unsubscribe_url is only supplied by UserNotifications#send_notification_email. Any other builder invocation with add_unsubscribe_link: true and no :unsubscribe_url option (other mailers, plugins, or future call sites — and the old spec case before it was patched in this same PR) will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument (or emit a broken literal `%{unsubscribe_url}` link) when building the email. The per-topic sentence should be a separate locale key used only when the URL is present.

No request specs for the unsubscribe controller action or route

The PR adds a new authenticated, state-mutating controller action (topics#unsubscribe) plus two new routes, but includes no request/controller specs covering: the redirect when the slug is missing/mismatched, the toggle behavior at each starting notification level, the nil-TopicUser case, access control for topics the user cannot see, and the logged-out redirect. The only test touched is the message_builder spec, so the most fragile new code (the toggling GET) ships untested.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' syntax is macOS-only and fails on Linux

The script uses `sed -i '' -E "..." "$ENV_FILE"`. On GNU/Linux sed, `-i ''` is interpreted as an empty file operand and the command fails, so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated on Linux dev machines. Also the relative `ENV_FILE="../.env"` depends on the caller's cwd. Use a portable check (e.g. `sed -i.bak`) or detect the platform.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the macOS-only `sed -i ''` syntax fails on Linux. The candidate also raises a separate point about the relative ENV_FILE path, but its main issue matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure thrown as generic Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential isn't found/owned, the handler throws a plain `Error('Credential not found or access denied')`, which tRPC surfaces as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) with the message leaking to the client. Cal.com's convention is to throw `TRPCError({ code: 'UNAUTHORIZED' | 'NOT_FOUND' })` so clients get correct status codes and no server error noise/alerting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the handler throws a generic Error for an auth/access failure, which tRPC turns into a 500, and that it should throw a TRPCError with a proper code instead. The candidate suggests UNAUTHORIZED or NOT_FOUND where the golden suggests FORBIDDEN, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp hardcoded to en-US and ignores user locale

The cache 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` instead of using the user's locale from `useLocale()`. All non-US users will see US-formatted dates (MM/DD/YYYY, 12-hour clock), inconsistent with the rest of the localized UI.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the date is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of the user's locale from useLocale.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache ownership check fails for delegated credentials

The handler authorizes the request with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. Delegation credentials often have `userId: null` (or an in-memory/negative id), so a user whose Google calendar is connected via a DelegationCredential will always get 'Credential not found or access denied' even though the UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) shows the 'Delete cached data' action for those credentials (hasCache is true when delegationCredentialId is set and canDisconnect is false). The user will always see 'Error deleting cache'. The check needs to account for delegated-to credentials the user has access to, or the UI must hide the delete action for them.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

After successfully deleting the cache via `trpc.viewer.calendars.deleteCache`, the component only calls `onSuccess?.()`. Unlike the disconnect mutation (which invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in onSettled), the delete-cache path never invalidates the `connectedCalendars` query. In the web wrapper `onChanged` is often undefined, so the UI will keep showing the old 'Cache Status / Last updated' timestamp (and the delete option) until an unrelated refetch happens, making the user think deletion didn't work.

Nested interactive elements / non-interactive DropdownMenuItem

`DropdownItem` (renders a `<button>`) is nested inside `DropdownMenuItem`, which itself renders a menu item element — this produces invalid nested interactive DOM and can break keyboard navigation and screen readers. The cache-status block is also rendered as a selectable menu item (line 84) that does nothing when clicked/activated, which is confusing for keyboard users; it should be a non-interactive label.

Deleting the cache does not repopulate it while webhooks remain active

`deleteCacheHandler` deletes all CalendarCache rows for the credential but leaves the Google webhook channel subscriptions intact and never triggers `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`. The cache is only repopulated on webhook events (which only fire on actual calendar changes) or the unwatch flow. For organizations relying on the calendar-cache feature, this means after deletion every availability check falls back to live Google freebusy API calls indefinitely until some calendar change occurs, defeating the purpose of the cache and risking Google API quota exhaustion. Deletion should trigger a re-fetch (as `unwatchCalendar` does with `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`).

No tests for new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds or deleteCache handler

The PR adds a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, including the groupBy/_max mapping and null handling), a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), and new enrichment logic in `connectedCalendarsHandler`, but includes no unit or e2e tests for any of them. In particular the credential-ownership check and the empty-credentialIds edge case are untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check compares UTC slot minutes against organizer-timezone working hours

In the new working-hours validation inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, `slotStartTime` is a UTC dayjs, so `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` yields minutes since midnight UTC. But `workingHour.startTime/endTime` (from `getUserAvailability` / `getAggregateWorkingHours`) are minutes since midnight in the organizer's timezone. For any organizer not in UTC (e.g. Asia/Kolkata in the test data, working hours 09:30–18:00 local), the comparison `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` uses the wrong clock, wrongly marking valid in-hours slots as unavailable or letting out-of-hours slots through. Additionally, `const end` is computed identically to `const start` (both from `slotStartTime`), so the `end > workingHour.endTime` condition never tests the slot's end time — the event length is not accounted for at all.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main point is the timezone mismatch. It also states that `const end` is computed from `slotStartTime` just like `start`, so the slot's end time is never checked. That is the same bug as the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object-identity comparison makes the unavailability-override check dead code

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the check `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false regardless of the underlying times. The intent (per the surrounding logic) was to detect a zero-length override, i.e. an override marking the whole day unavailable (start === end). Such 'blocked day' overrides will not be recognized by this branch; instead they fall through to the subsequent `slotEndTime.isBefore(...)` checks, which for an empty range will mark every slot as outside the override and the day will incorrectly become unavailable (or available depending on order) — in any case the special-cased behavior can never trigger and is dead code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: comparing two dayjs objects with === checks reference identity, so the result is always false. The candidate pins this to the same line and adds that the branch is therefore dead code.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check entirely

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, once a slot is found to be on a day with a date override and inside the override window, the function returns `true` immediately (`if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }`) without ever evaluating the `busy` array. This means that for fixed hosts (the primary path this PR adds, where `checkIfIsAvailable` is the only busy-time filter), any existing booking or calendar busy time that falls inside a date-override window will be reported as available. The attendee can be shown (and attempt to book) a slot where the host already has a meeting. The override should restrict the time window, not bypass conflict checking.

Date overrides that cross midnight in the invitee timezone are silently dropped

The new override computation converts the override start/end to minutes since midnight in the invitee timezone (`dayjs(...).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`). `hour()` wraps at 24, so an override such as 23:00–01:00 (invitee time) produces `startTime: 1380, endTime: 60`. `buildSlots` then skips this timeframe via the `if (start >= end) continue;` guard, so the override disappears entirely instead of splitting into two ranges. The previous code had the same wrap problem, but this rewrite was the opportunity to fix it; users with overnight overrides will see their normal working hours applied (or no availability) instead of the override.

Override-day matching compares organizer-local date against UTC slot date

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares the organizer-local calendar date of the override start with the UTC calendar date of the slot. For organizers in non-UTC timezones, slots in the first hours of a UTC day (or last hours) belong to a different local day, so the override-day detection is off by one day for those slots. Slots just after midnight UTC on the override day will not be treated as override-day slots (and vice versa), producing wrong availability at day boundaries.

No test for the fixed-host date override in a round-robin team event

The PR's headline fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected in round-robin events (issue #8207), but the added test only covers a single-user event with a date override and a different invitee timezone. There is no test with a ROUND_ROBIN event containing an `isFixed` host with a date override plus a non-fixed host, so the main code path added in `getSchedule` (`fixedHosts.every(...)` with date overrides) and the buggy busy-time bypass it introduces are not exercised by any test.

DST offset computed once from override start may be wrong for override end

The offset applied to the override is derived from a single instant (`override.start`): `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()`. If the override range spans a DST transition (possible for multi-hour or multi-day overrides), the end time is shifted by the start instant's offset, misplacing the end of the availability window by the DST delta. The offset should be evaluated at the respective instant for both start and end.

Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (sending 'guests added' emails and calendar updates for an event that no longer exists), and for seat-based event types the attendee count can be pushed past `seatsPerTimeSlot`, corrupting the seat invariant.
